💡 Key Takeaways
  • When American entrepreneur Jeffrey Tucker told Bitcoiners to stop dreaming about Bitcoin becoming the world's most valuable asset, Strategy co-founder Michael Saylor responded with the example of a gold-backed banknote.
  • Industry observers note that "Give it up, Bitcoiners.
  • It has been revealed that tucker argued that Bitcoiners had brought the criticism upon themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When American entrepreneur Jeffrey Tucker told Bitcoiners to stop dreaming about Bitcoin becoming the world's most valuable asset, Strategy co-founder Michael Saylor responded with the example of a gold-backed banknote.

Industry observers note that "Give it up, Bitcoiners. There is no such thing as money that is not used in exchange," Tucker wrote on X.

It has been revealed that tucker argued that Bitcoiners had brought the criticism upon themselves. They made the mistake of thinking they could simply declare Bitcoin a store of value and that would somehow make it one. That is not how it works, according to Tucker. He argued that nothing in the history of money supports this idea.

According to recent reports, in his response, Saylor started with an example involving a bakery. Suppose someone buys bread at a bakery. They pay for the bread with a gold-backed banknote. The baker can use that banknote to pay the miller. The miller can use it to pay the farmer. All three transactions could be completed using the same banknote, while the gold stays in the vault.

According to recent reports, @jeffreytucker Jeffrey, a gold-backed banknote could pay the baker, the miller, and the farmer while the gold stayed in the vault. Today people pay in dollars and save in gold, stocks, and real estate. Bitcoin is competing for those savings.

In the second part of his response, Saylor made an argument familiar to anyone who gets paid in dollars.

It has been revealed that sure, you can use dollars to buy groceries. However, you can still decide to keep some of your wealth in stocks, gold, or real estate.

Industry observers note that "Today people pay in dollars and save in gold, stocks, and real estate. Bitcoin is competing for those savings," Saylor wrote.

This last point was less ambitious than the claim Tucker was pushing back against.

Tucker was talking about Bitcoin becoming the world's most valuable asset.

Saylor, meanwhile, was making a simpler argument about where people choose to keep their savings.

Sources indicate that however, Saylor's gold analogy raises an interesting question for Tucker. In Saylor's example, gold is still relevant to the purchase of bread because it backs the banknote the baker accepts.

However, in his modern examples, someone who chooses to save in stocks isn't necessarily concerned about whether their local bakery accepts stocks as payment.

For Tucker, it's all about how the customer pays for a loaf of bread. For Saylor, it's about what the baker does with the money after selling it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Given the rise in the acceptance of digital assets, the ASEAN+3 member countries have agreed to establish a dedicated working group to advance discussions on cross-border digital payments and regulatory approaches to digital assets.

The decision was unveiled in the Co-chairs’ Statement following the ASEAN+3 Finance and Central Bank Deputies’ Meeting held in Kyoto, Japan recently.

Here, the initiative aims to strengthen regional financial cooperation by improving payment connectivity and encouraging discussions on how crypto should be regulated across participating economies.

In fact, it also marks a step towards greater coordination among Asian financial authorities as digital assets and blockchain-based financial services continue to expand.

Industry observers note that to make this successful, the proposed working group aims to operate under the newly established AMRO Cross-Border Digital Payments Program. Under the same, they will provide a dedicated platform for ASEAN+3 economies to discuss retail and wholesale payment connectivity, alongside regulatory approaches to digital assets.

Industry observers note that this is particularly key because cross-border payments remain fragmented across different financial systems. Needless to say, differences in payment infrastructure, regulations, and compliance requirements make international transactions slower and more expensive.

However, with greater coordination, participating economies could explore inter-operable payment systems and more consistent regulatory approaches.

Interestingly, the development also comes amid broader efforts by governments and financial regulators to address the growing influence of cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and tokenized assets.

One prominent example is the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) framework. It became fully applicable on 30th December 2024, following the introduction of stablecoin-specific provisions in June 2024.

According to recent reports, for those unaware, MiCA establishes common rules for crypto-asset issuers and service providers, covering authorization, transparency, investor protection, and market conduct. Its implementation has provided a regulatory benchmark for other jurisdictions considering comprehensive crypto frameworks.

Recent findings suggest that south Africa is another example of this shift. In August 2026, the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) and National Treasury proposed an activity-based reporting framework for cross-border crypto transactions.

According to recent reports, the proposal focuses on identifying and monitoring transactions that could facilitate capital flight, illegal financial flows, or regulatory circumvention. Rather than classifying crypto assets as official currency, it seeks to bring their cross-border movement under closer financial safeguards.

Recent findings suggest that on the other hand, the United States has faced setbacks in establishing similar regulatory clarity. The proposed Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act failed to advance in the Senate on 15th September, receiving 49 votes in favor and 50 against. it was short of the 60 votes required to proceed.

Its failure has left the U.S without the proposed comprehensive federal market structure framework, potentially putting it behind jurisdictions such as the E.U in providing regulatory certainty. However, the SEC and CFTC continue to pursue regulatory initiatives under their existing authority.

Against this backdrop, ASEAN+3’s latest decision is the latest in the world’s global regulatory discussion/efforts.

Bob Hope at Home: 10 Photos of the Comic’s Life Behind the Curtain

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA.
  • Sources indicate that born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings.
  • Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, though Bob Hope was born in England, he fell in love with the USA. “Sometimes I do my best to hide it, but I’ve got a real crush on America,” he wrote in his 1990 memoir, Don’t Shoot, It’s Only Me. “Nobody ever had a girl like her. Nobody ever gave me as much affection, as much honor, or as much real estate.”.

Sources indicate that born Leslie Townes Hope in Eltham, London, on May 29, 1903, the future comedian and actor came from humble beginnings. His family had little money and moved often throughout his childhood. After he found success on stage and it came time to raise his own brood, Hope put down roots in California. Across Toluca Lake and Palm Springs, the star’s homes offered a place to escape the limelight, spend time with his wife and four kids, entertain very famous guests, and indulge in his love of golf.

Below, we’ve rounded up 10 photos of Hope at home, from his early family life to the residence where he died at age 100.

Hope (bottom right) at the family estate in Cleveland. The comic’s parents William Henry Hope and Avis Townes Hope are on the porch in the background. Hope was 20 years old at the time of the picture.

Hope and his family moved from London to the United States when he was four. In this 1923 photo, he’s pictured with friends and members of the Hope clan at their Cleveland home. Because money was tight, the family took in boarders to supplement Hope’s father’s income, according to the Library of Congress. In his 1954 memoir, Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope recalls his early days in Cleveland. “The first place we lived by ourselves was Standiforth Court,” he wrote. “We were always on the move. We lived at 2029 Euclid. After that we moved behind the Cleveland Express barns…. It was a long walk between the barns and our house. And if we got home after dark, it was scary…. Next we lived at 1925 East 105th, then at 1913, then at 2029—all on Euclid. We didn’t move very far, only to bigger houses which had more room for roomers.”.

Hope and his wife Dolores at home in the 1940s.

Hope married Dolores DeFina in 1934, and the couple adopted their first child, a daughter named Linda, in 1939. That same year, the comic bought a five-acre former walnut grove in Los Angeles’s Toluca Lake neighborhood at 10346 Moorpark Street. He transformed the property into a lavish French Revival estate, featuring a 14,876-square-foot main house with eight bedrooms and eight bathrooms; a two-bedroom, two-bathroom guesthouse; a staff residence; and a pool.

Hope and his grandfather catch up over tea.

In this 1943 photo, Hope is pictured at home with his “Grandpop.” As a young boy in London, Hope lived with his family in a house his grandfather had built. “Grandpop had built a row of houses in Eltham. We lived in one of them. They were put together like stone battleships,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. After moving to the United States, his grandfather went on to build churches in Cleveland and Detroit. Hope reunited with him during a return trip to England in 1939—the star’s first visit since moving across the pond as a child. He recalls the occasion in his memoir, writing that “It wasn’t until I went back to England in 1939 that I got to know [Grandpop]. It was the first time I’d been there since I was four. The English papers reported: ‘One-time shoeshine boy and ironmonger’s assistant comes home.’ The English are supposed to be conservative and not given to exaggeration, but they hooked one there. How could I have been a shoeshine boy or ironmonger’s assistant when I was only four when I left there?”.

Hope and family at home in the 1940s.

Back in California, Hope and his wife continued to grow their family. They adopted three more children: Anthony, born in 1940, and twins William and Eleanora, born in 1946. In this circa 1940s photo, the family of six is pictured at home. In Have Tux, Will Travel, Hope reflects on the choice to adopt. “No matter how strongly I feel about the word ‘family,’ Dolores feels even more deeply about it,” he writes. “When we found out that she couldn’t bear children, she began to bend my ear about adoption.” They welcomed their children through The Cradle, an adoption agency in Evanston, Illinois. “Of the five thousand, four hundred and nine babies that The Cradle has placed, there are eight Cradle babies out here in Hollywood,” he continues. “The Hopes are proud to be Cradle parents. I wish I could really tell you what The Cradle means to me here in Hollywood, where all day long the talk is box-office and autographs and premieres and who’ll get the Oscar. ‘The town of make-believe,’ they call it, but don’t get the idea everything is make-believe in Hollywood. There's nothing make-believe about our children. They are real.”.

Hope enjoys some family time in the living room with Dolores and two of their children.

Hope’s Toluca Lake estate was more than a family retreat; it was also a gathering place for celebrities and politicians, including Bing Crosby and Richard Nixon. When the property went on the market for $27.5 million in 2013, listing agent Jade Mills said, “[Hope’s] daughter, Linda Hope, would often peek down the grand staircase to see who was coming. She once spoke to Lucie Arnaz and Maria Cooper about doing a book about watching celebrities come and go called ‘Seen From the Landing.’”.

The home was “always impressively staffed,” Mills continued. “A full-time cook, butler, estate manager, and two housekeepers manned the property on a daily basis, while additional staff was hired for large receptions.”.

Hope, Dolores, and their four kids pose at home in 1958.

In this 1958 photo, Hope and the family pose for a photo on the stairs. In Have Tux, Will Travel, the comic gushes about his wife as a mother. “Dolores has a wise and loving touch with our children,” he writes. “I’m lost in admiration of the job she has done with them, and with the job she’s done with keeping me in line. A lot of children whose fathers are in show business grow up too precocious, too wise, too fresh, too unfunny. That’s not true of our four. Dolores sees to that. She also sees to it that they’re having a devout rearing.”.

The family is shown here opening Christmas presents in 1964.

In a recent development, hope was determined to give his children space at home. “When our kids began to grow up, we fixed up a play room for them and gave them rooms of their own,” he writes in Have Tux, Will Travel. “While we were at it, Dolores and I decided to redo the whole house. We tore out one entire downstairs wall and put in glass, so no matter where we are, we can look out at the garden and enjoy the California sun—if it shows up.”.

While his home workspace was connected to the residence, it was its own separate world. “My office adjoins my house,” he writes. “It’s a different project, separate and distinct from our house. In fact, it’s on a different property. It was put up (and is owned) by Hope Enterprises. But it’s handy. The people I want to see on business can walk in and out without disturbing anybody…. It’s a nice set-up.”.

Hope was an avid golfer in his free time.

Hope was an avid golfer and built a one-hole golf course at his home in Toluca Lake, where he’s pictured here in this 1990-era photo. He once even remarked that he considered golf to be his real job. “Golf is my profession,” he said, per ESPN. “Entertainment is just a sideline. I tell jokes to pay my greens fees.” The outlet further reported that he played more than 2,000 courses all over the world and golfed with everyone from Crosby to Dwight Eisenhower and Bill Clinton. “I’ve played all over the world, which means there isn’t a country with a course in which I haven’t three-putted,” Hope said.

Hope and Dolores at home in Palm Springs.

While Toluca Lake served as the family’s primary residence, Hope’s most iconic home was arguably his Palm Springs estate, where he and Dolores are pictured here in 1991. Designed by famed architect John Lautner, the 24,000-square-foot estate featured 10 bedrooms, dramatic arches, and a statement curved roof. The futuristic design closely resembled a spaceship. Hope once joked, “Well, at least when they come down from Mars they’ll know where to go.”.

It has been revealed that the home’s construction, however, was plagued by setbacks. According to the Los Angeles Times, when building began in the early ’70s, the structure caught on fire and burned down. The project was subsequently delayed for five years, during which time the couple’s interior designer, Arthur Elrod, was killed in a car accident. Dolores then took over the design duties. Lautner’s protégé Helena Arahuete recalled Dolores’s vision: “She wanted everything very ornamented, very rich—you know, gold and pink and black and mirrors everywhere.” Inspired by her friends Walter and Leonore Annenberg’s home, which had a pink roof, Dolores requested that their curved roof be covered in pink terra-cotta gunite.

According to recent reports, in 1991, at his Palm Springs pad, Hope hosted “Bob Hope’s Yellow Ribbon Party,” a homecoming celebration for U.S. troops. The soiree included celebrity guest appearances by Brooke Shields, Patti LaBelle, Jimmy Stewart, and former President Gerald Ford and his wife, Betty.

According to recent reports, hope died at home in Toluca Lake in 2003 at the age of 100. The estate remained in the family until Dolores’s death in 2011, after which it was listed for $50 million. LA businessman Ron Burkle purchased the star’s Palm Springs pad in 2016, and two years later, added Hope’s Toluca Lake residence to his real estate portfolio.

What Is the Best Type of Yogurt? We Narrowed It Down to the World’s 8 Healthiest.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that EVERYBODY LOVE YOGURT.
  • "Most of the world is lactose intolerant and has been for thousands and thousands of years," says Robert Hutkins, PhD, a professor of food microbiology at the University of Nebraska.
  • Whether you need help digesting lactose or not, the latest research suggests that yogurt has wide-ranging benefits, from enhancing gut health to improving blood sugar control to maybe even reducing your risk of an early death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that EVERYBODY LOVE YOGURT. Okay, maybe not everyone, but there's a reason yogurt has been a dietary staple in dozens of countries for centuries. Yogurt doesn't spoil as fast as milk, yet still delivers milk's nutrients—protein, calcium, potassium, magnesium—without the same risk of, um, certain GI concerns.

"Most of the world is lactose intolerant and has been for thousands and thousands of years," says Robert Hutkins, PhD, a professor of food microbiology at the University of Nebraska. "Humans figured out that even if they were lactose intolerant, they could still consume cultured milks because the culture helps degrade the lactose before it gets to the colon and gets fermented by gas-producing microbes.".

Whether you need help digesting lactose or not, the latest research suggests that yogurt has wide-ranging benefits, from enhancing gut health to improving blood sugar control to maybe even reducing your risk of an early death.

From Europe to Asia to Africa, all yogurt starts with the same basic ingredients: milk and good bacteria. But no two types are exactly alike. Here's what to know before your next grocery run.

Traditional Greek yogurt is strained through a cheesecloth to remove excess fluid. Yogurt factories use centrifuges or special filters instead. What's left behind is a thick, smooth yogurt with a slightly acidic flavor and a concentrated source of nutrients, including about 18 grams of protein per 6-ounce container.

Some food makers add thickeners as a shortcut, so check the label for a simple ingredient list of milk, cream, and yogurt cultures. "The products with thickeners added have a different texture, a little bit more gumminess," says Molly Kimball, RD, CSSD, a dietitian based in Louisiana. Swap in Greek yogurt for sour cream or mayo, or stir it into guacamole—the lactic acid slows down the oxidation that turns avocados brown.

Technically considered a soft cheese, skyr is strained like Greek yogurt to produce something firm yet creamy. It's usually made with skim milk, yielding yogurt with slightly more protein than Greek yogurt: about 19 grams of protein per 6 ounces. Use skyr to make dips hearty enough to stand up to cut vegetables (or chips). Or stir it into bolognese to impart a velvety texture and an extra boost of protein.

This yogurt variety isn't strained, so it has a thinner texture and less protein than its Greek or Icelandic cousins: about 6 grams per 6 ounces. Traditional Bulgarian yogurt gets its signature sharp flavor from high concentrations of the aptly named Lactobacillus Bulgaricus bacteria, which produce lactic acid. Kimball recommends blending Bulgarian yogurt into smoothies to add a tanginess that counterbalances sweeter ingredients.

Most yogurts are fermented in large vats. As yogurt bacteria digest milk, they produce a wide variety of metabolites, including gel-like substances called exopolysaccharides. Then the yogurt is pumped into the smaller containers we snag at the grocery store.

It has been revealed that with French-style yogurt, the milk and bacterial cultures are poured into cups earlier, before the microbes multiply. "That gives you a more custardy product because it hasn't gone through this pumping phase that disturbs the gel," states Hutkins. Inside a 6-ounce cup of French-style yogurt, you'll find about 5 grams of protein. To try it the French way, eat your yogurt for dessert, alone or paired with a little honey or jam.

Industry observers note that this tangy, thin, pourable yogurt is fermented with kefir grains–gelatinous clusters that contain milk proteins and up to 50 bacterial and yeast species. During fermentation, these yeasts can leave behind traces of alcohol and carbon dioxide, or fizz. However, many mass-produced kefirs use standardized starter cultures instead to maintain consistent product quality and keep the alcohol concentration low enough to sell in grocery stores.

Industry observers note that kimball suggests drinking plain kefir, Russian or otherwise. It packs about 8 grams of protein per cup. If you can't handle the sour flavor, balance it with a teaspoon or less of maple syrup or a few drops of stevia or monk fruit. If you want a flavored variety, pick one with no more than 5 grams of added sugar.

It has been revealed that sweet and mildly acidic, dahi is the key ingredient in Indian staples like lassi–a yogurt drink often flavored with mango, spices, or rosewater–and raita, the sauce that cools your mouth when you order your vindaloo extra hot. Some dahi varieties contain Leuconostoc, bacteria that produce a metabolite called diacetyl that imparts a buttery flavor. Each six-ounce serving of dahi packs about 7 grams of protein.

Drinkable like kefir, laban is sour but smooth and contains about 5 grams of protein per six ounces. Strain it in a colander or cheesecloth to make labneh, a thick, soft, yogurt-like cheese traditionally smeared on sandwiches and stacked on mezze platters.

This drinkable yogurt is often thicker than fermented milk beverages. Its mix of cultures, which hail mostly from the Lactobacillusgenus, imparts a moderately acidic flavor with subtle buttery notes. Amasi packs about 6 grams of protein per six ounces. It's traditionally eaten with maize or sorghum porridge, especially at breakfast.

Julie Stewart is a writer and content strategist whose work has also appeared in Health, and Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Vice, and Shape.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home » Trendsetter News » Analyst: Ripple’s Growth Doesn’t Guarantee $10 XRP.

Ripple’s expansion alone won’t send XRP to $10, a popular wealth coach states.

A $10 XRP would imply a circulating market value of roughly $630 billion, not simply another rally on Ripple announcements.

That is the central argument from Dr. Kamilah Stevenson, a wealth coach whose latest YouTube video episode examines why the tech giant’s institutional expansion has not translated into the token price many holders expected.

Industry observers note that using approximately 63 billion XRP in circulation, Stevenson argues that reaching that XRP valuation requires more than partnerships and regulatory milestones. It requires sustained demand to own the token, rather than merely move money through it.

Sources indicate that stevenson separates Ripple’s corporate performance, adoption of its products, demand for XRP and the token’s market price. Those categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable: a customer using Ripple’s custody services or stablecoin does not necessarily need XRP.

Recent findings suggest that even payments routed through XRP may generate limited lasting demand. In the process she describes, a payment provider buys the token, transfers it and sells it into the destination currency within seconds, allowing the same inventory to support repeated transactions.

“Major payment numbers alone don’t automatically push the price up,” Dr. Stevenson states. The more consequential question is how much XRP participants need to keep available between transactions.

It has been revealed that market makers may hold inventory to support larger payment flows, creating a potential link between usage and ownership. Still, the video does not quantify how much additional inventory those flows would require.

Dr. Kamilah Stevenson cites roughly 1.19 billion XRP held by ETFs and about 473 million held by Evernorth, a organization established to accumulate XRP. Those are figures presented in the video, rather than independently verified current totals.

Her distinction is useful: XRP-backed fund holdings represent direct token ownership, while the national trust bank approval she attributes to Ripple does not itself require institutions to purchase XRP.

Sources indicate that supply remains part of the calculation. Stevenson puts Ripple’s escrow holdings at around 31 billion XRP, with up to one billion released monthly and unused amounts returned to escrow. An unlock is therefore not equivalent to an immediate market sale.

Recent findings suggest that the sharper test is whether an announcement creates incremental buying, how long those tokens stay held and whether new supply offsets that demand. Dr. Stevenson remains bullish, but the adoption figures she discusses do not establish when XRP reaches $10.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • JPMorgan may have to spend between $500 million and $1 billion to build out its Bitcoin business, according to SkyBridge Capital's Anthony Scaramucci.
  • It's JPMorgan's willingness to spend money serving Bitcoin clients that tells us more about its aims than CEO Jamie Dimon calling the cryptocurrency a "pet rock.".
  • Scaramucci also claimed that a research note circulating within JPMorgan's private bank recommended allocating 10% of a portfolio to Bitcoin, describing it as potentially the most undervalued asset of the next decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JPMorgan may have to spend between $500 million and $1 billion to build out its Bitcoin business, according to SkyBridge Capital's Anthony Scaramucci.

It's JPMorgan's willingness to spend money serving Bitcoin clients that tells us more about its aims than CEO Jamie Dimon calling the cryptocurrency a "pet rock.".

Scaramucci also claimed that a research note circulating within JPMorgan's private bank recommended allocating 10% of a portfolio to Bitcoin, describing it as potentially the most undervalued asset of the next decade.

In a recent development, scaramucci did not provide a timeline for the spending estimate. Neither the estimate nor the research note could be independently verified through publicly available JPMorgan documents.

"Know the difference between what people say and what they do with their money," Scaramucci wrote on X.

Scaramucci was referring to what it might cost JPMorgan to develop a business serving Bitcoin clients.

The 10% allocation recommendation, meanwhile, concerns how much of a client's portfolio should be invested in Bitcoin.

If you have a $1 million portfolio, that would mean allocating $100,000 to Bitcoin.

It doesn't mean JPMorgan is buying Bitcoin and adding it to its own balance sheet.

This distinction matters because a bank can profit from clients who want Bitcoin exposure even if its CEO believes they're making a bad investment.

If JPMorgan were willing to spend hundreds of millions of dollars serving Bitcoin clients, assuming Scaramucci's numbers are correct, that would suggest the bank expects substantial demand for these services.

We have a specific example of what JPMorgan already offers in a securities filing dated Nov. 24.

The filing covers $300,000 worth of notes linked to BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, priced by JPMorgan's financing subsidiary.

Someone who invests $1,000 in these notes could receive $1,300 if the ETF closes at or above its initial price on the observation date in November 2027.

However, investors also risk losing some or all of their principal.

It's a product JPMorgan created around a financial position that clients might want to take: where will this Bitcoin ETF be trading in a year's time?

Scaramucci suggested that Dimon has regulators in mind when he publicly criticizes Bitcoin.

"He's a smart guy. He knows he has to go before regulators and say the right things," Scaramucci said.

According to Scaramucci's interpretation, Dimon can publicly dismiss Bitcoin to maintain a conservative stance while JPMorgan develops products for clients who want exposure to the cryptocurrency.

However, this is Scaramucci's interpretation of Dimon's motives.

Dimon's own public explanation has been more straightforward.

In a CNBC interview at Davos in January 2024, Dimon described Bitcoin as a "pet rock.".

At JPMorgan's investor day in May 2025, Dimon raised concerns about leverage and illicit activity involving Bitcoin.

But he also made it clear that customers could buy Bitcoin and see their holdings reflected on JPMorgan statements. At the time, he mentioned the bank would leave custody to third parties.

"I defend your right to buy Bitcoin," Dimon remarked.

Against this backdrop, the research note Scaramucci described would be particularly significant, assuming his claims are accurate.

Dimon has already explained why JPMorgan would allow customers to buy Bitcoin.

But recommending that clients allocate one dollar out of every ten in their portfolios to Bitcoin would be a much bigger step.

The November securities filing reveals that JPMorgan is willing to offer products providing Bitcoin exposure.

However, it has not been independently confirmed that JPMorgan's private bankers are recommending such a substantial allocation to their clients.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wallets linked to Abraxas Capital received another 1,700 Bitcoin [BTC] from Kraken, worth roughly $103 million. The transfers, reported on 27th November, arrived in batches of 700 BTC and 1,000 BTC.

The latest Abraxas Bitcoin withdrawals brought the six-day tally across Kraken and Binance to about 21,500 BTC. On-chain tracker EmberCN valued those transfers at $1.285 billion.

Lookonchain called the latest transfers a purchase.

By 27th November, Arkham had tracked about 28,982 BTC across addresses it attributed to Abraxas Capital’s Heka Funds.

Lookonchain first flagged Abraxas cutting shorts on 16th November, the day Lighter reported an API key leak. The tracker tentatively linked Abraxas to the affected Lighter account.

Abraxas Capital has now withdrawn all its funds from Hyperliquid.

According to recent reports, by 25th November, Abraxas had pulled its remaining funds from Hyperliquid. It also sold 219,081 HYPE and bought 4,230 Ethereum [ETH].

Sources indicate that additionally, on-chain researcher MLM described the Hyperliquid positions as part of Elysium Global Arbitrage Fund’s market-neutral strategy. The estimated profit was around $530 – $552.49 million.

According to one X user, Abraxas “pulled the funds to buy Bitcoin.” Another suggested,.

My guess is the shorts were moved to exchanges.

In fact, Hyperliquid records revealed that the shorts had closed. If those shorts hedged Bitcoin and Abraxas let them lapse, its net BTC exposure could rise without another purchase.

While those wallets received Bitcoin [BTC], recent holders have been sitting on heavy paper losses.

Industry observers note that on 26th November, Alphractal’s STH Unrealized Profit/Loss Ratio hit 0.01. With a reading of 0.01, the ratio indicated how far underwater recent holders were at press time.

In a recent development, in essence, it implied that short-term holders’ unrealized losses were roughly 100 times their unrealized profits, with Bitcoin’s price near $60,500. According to Alphractal Founder and CEO Joao Wedson, such extremes have “often accompanied market bottom formations.”.

Bitcoin’s turbulent week has created a $16 billion opportunity for a short squeeze

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that bitcoin is trying to recover after a volatile week.
  • Bitcoin traded at $61,436 at 13:09 UTC on Nov.
  • Bitcoin climbed above $64,000 on Monday following Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, which also drove the chipmaker's shares 31% higher and helped major US equity indices register their strongest sessions in more than a year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that bitcoin is trying to recover after a volatile week. If buying carries it higher, leveraged short sellers forced to close their positions could add to the rebound.

Bitcoin traded at $61,436 at 13:09 UTC on Nov. 27, down 0.2% over the previous seven days, according to CryptoSlate’s Bitcoin price tracker.

Bitcoin climbed above $64,000 on Monday following Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, which also drove the chipmaker's shares 31% higher and helped major US equity indices register their strongest sessions in more than a year.

However, the cryptocurrency surrendered its gains within hours and subsequently fell below $58,000 as concerns about the sustainability of the AI investment boom resurfaced.

According to recent reports, glassnode’s market analysis described Bitcoin’s reversal as an early sign that investors were selling into strength. The Nasdaq came under pressure a day later. However, global markets showed renewed signs of recovery on Friday. S&P 500 futures rose nearly 2%, Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 2.8%, and Dow Jones futures gained 655 points ahead of a shortened US trading session following Thanksgiving.

Equities across Asia and Europe also advanced, providing a more favorable backdrop for Bitcoin as bearish bets against the digital asset accumulate.

CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost noted that Bitcoin's price struggles this week have pushed its short-term holder market value-to-realized value (MVRV) ratio to 0.85, approaching the 0.81 reading recorded during the market's July 1 downturn.

The indicator measures the relationship between the market value of Bitcoin held by short-term investors and their aggregate acquisition cost, providing insight into the financial pressure facing recent buyers.

The ratio peaked at 1.18 on Sept. 22, when short-term holders were sitting on average unrealized profits of approximately 18%.

The subsequent decline has erased those gains, leaving the cohort with average unrealized losses of around 15% and an estimated cost basis of $71,600.

Darkfost remarked similar periods of financial stress have coincided with past Bitcoin bottoms, when prices traded below recent buyers’ acquisition costs.

Alphractal CEO Joao Wedson identified similar patterns across previous Bitcoin halving cycles, noting that the broader MVRV ratio's historical trajectories have remained remarkably consistent despite differences in the magnitude of price fluctuations.

According to Wedson, the current cycle's valuation trajectory suggests Bitcoin may be approaching the final stages of one of its strongest accumulation opportunities.

“History may not repeat itself perfectly, but the cyclical behavior of Bitcoin remains difficult to ignore.”.

At the UTC afternoon price, Bitcoin would need to rise about 16.5% to reach that estimated cost basis.

Meanwhile, the derivatives market has developed a substantial liquidation imbalance that could accelerate such a recovery if buying demand returns.

It has been revealed that cryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju’s Nov. 26 Bitcoin liquidation map estimated $16 billion in potential short liquidations across prices from $60,000 to $100,000, against less than $5 billion in potential long liquidations below that range.

Reconstructed from approximate $500-step screenshot bars, with cumulative amounts rounded to $0.1 billion. Long exposure falls toward zero as BTC price rises to $60,000; short exposure accumulates above $60,000. The short-side plateau follows the source screenshot, not verified future outcomes. Figures are model estimates; underlying CryptoQuant CSV was unavailable.

Sources indicate that source: CryptoQuant — BTC Estimated Liquidation Levels, screenshot supplied Nov. 27, 2026.

A move through nearby resistance would still leave much of the $60,000 to $100,000 range untested.

“Short squeeze fuel is piling up for the next rally, imo.”.

An upward price move could force leveraged traders betting against Bitcoin to close their positions, adding buying pressure and potentially accelerating the cryptocurrency's recovery.

It has been revealed that cryptoSlate tracked a similar short-squeeze setup on Nov. 20, when a sell-off left a large cluster of shorts vulnerable to a price rebound. In the latest figures supplied by Bitunix, open interest rose while trading volume fell.

Analysts at crypto exchange Bitunix told CryptoSlate that Bitcoin's trading volume had declined nearly 47% over the preceding 24 hours, while liquidations fell approximately 69%.

Open interest, however, rose 1.2% to 1.5% over the same period, indicating that outstanding derivatives exposure grew despite the slowdown in trading activity.

Meanwhile, cumulative volume delta (CVD), which measures the difference between aggressive buying and selling, remained negative across both spot and futures markets.

Bitunix noted Bitcoin's ability to rebound despite negative CVD suggests that buyers are absorbing selling pressure, although aggressive buying demand has yet to materialize.

Recent findings suggest that the analysts identified $62,000 as Bitcoin's immediate resistance level, followed by a more concentrated supply zone between $62,400 and $62,640. A sustained break above these levels could expose nearby bearish positions to liquidation, providing the initial momentum needed to trigger a broader short squeeze.

Conversely, Bitunix warned that renewed dollar strength and a breakdown below $61,050 could send Bitcoin back toward the $60,350 to $60,600 support zone.

Friday's recovery in global equities provides a favorable backdrop for testing those resistance levels. Whether Bitcoin can sustain that momentum will depend on buyers absorbing the overhead supply that has repeatedly frustrated its recovery this week.

Latest Update: The 21 Best Adam Driver Movies, Ranked

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that LET’S SWIFTLY CUT to the chase: Adam Driver is a good actor.
  • Recent findings suggest that some may still think of Driver, who this month teams up with director James Gray for one of his best roles ever in the crime drama Paper Tiger, as Adam Sackler, the overly emotional Brooklyn boyfriend of Lena Dunham in Girls (a role for which he was nominated for three Emmys).
  • It has been revealed that driver has emerged in recent years as someone who works almost exclusively with elite, top-notch directors, headlining projects from the likes of Scorsese and Michael Mann as well as Spike Lee and Ridley Scott (just to name a few).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that LET’S SWIFTLY CUT to the chase: Adam Driver is a good actor. That’s probably an understatement to say the least; if Martin Scorsese, of all people, refers to someone as “one of the finest, if not the finest actor of his generation,” well, then, yeah, they’re probably pretty good.

Recent findings suggest that some may still think of Driver, who this month teams up with director James Gray for one of his best roles ever in the crime drama Paper Tiger, as Adam Sackler, the overly emotional Brooklyn boyfriend of Lena Dunham in Girls (a role for which he was nominated for three Emmys). But while he was obviously stellar in his breakthrough role on HBO’s hit comedy, it’s clear that he’s come a significant way in the time since first coming through to the public consciousness.

It has been revealed that driver has emerged in recent years as someone who works almost exclusively with elite, top-notch directors, headlining projects from the likes of Scorsese and Michael Mann as well as Spike Lee and Ridley Scott (just to name a few). He frequently shows his comedy (or, maybe dramedy) chops working with Noah Baumbach.

He’s also, of course, earned his presence on the blockbuster scene: while opinions abound with regard to the Star Wars sequel trilogy, it’d be hard for anyone to deny the intensity with which Driver dominates the screen as the main villain of those films.

For someone whose film career has only been going for about a decade, Driver has a remarkable resume and, having been nominated for a pair of Oscars already, accomplished a huge amount. As he continues to add more and more exciting projects to his ledger—he’s recently joined the cast of Marvel’s new X-Men movie— we wanted to rank the very best roles Driver has had so far.

Here are the best films of Adam Driver, ranked.

In one of his first leading roles, Driver gave audiences a taste of the intense leading man he would eventually become as one half of a deeply troubled couple (with a newborn child) in Hungry Hearts.

One thing we haven’t gotten enough of—in the post-Girls era—is Driver showing off his full comedy chops. In What If, a rom-com where he stars alongside Daniel Radcliffe, Zoe Kazan, and Mackenzie Davis, he gets to have a whole lot of fun as a romantic co-lead (and yell about having sex and eating nachos).

White Noise marked Driver’s fifth collaboration with writer/director Noah Baumbach. And while the movie didn’t wind up getting the Oscar love that it may have aspired for, it still found Driver giving a committed and intense—if deeply strange—performance. Fans of Don DeLillo's book upon which the film is based probably enjoyed what he brought to the table here.

One of the hallmarks of Driver’s recent career is working with as many legendary directors as he can possibly fit into his schedule. That includes three movies with indie king Jim Jarmusch; Father Mother Sister Brother cast Driver as a key piece of a striking ensemble, and delivered one of his most naturalistic and honest recent performances.

According to recent reports, speaking of legendary directors, Driver took the lead in Megalopolis, the maximalist, long-in-the-works sci-fi epic from Francis Ford Coppola (of The Godfather and Apocalypse Now fame), as an urban planner or architect of some sort in a bizarre future world. The movie is kind of a massive disaster, but Driver, as always, brings his all (with some legendary line-readings included). It’s hard to say it’s good, but you certainly can’t look away—and it’s clearly an experience Driver wanted. An crucial touchstone for his career in any regard.

It has been revealed that megalopolis is not streaming anywhere or available on physical media. You are on your own with this one—if you find it, let me know.

In a movie full of larger-than-life, outrageous characters (and even more outrageous accents), Driver manages to somewhat keep House of Gucci on the rails. He plays Ridley Scott’s Maurizio Gucci, and while he, too, has an absurd accent, it somehow winds up being the most grounded and reasoned performance in the whole film. This movie is camp, but Driver winds up playing it pretty straight—which mostly works.

In a recent development, driver’s first collaboration with Noah Baumbach came as Lev, a dude who comes in and out of the life of Greta Gerwig’s titular character as she flails her way through her 20s. This light and fun character feels almost like the opposite of Driver’s intense turn in another coming-of-age-in-NYC-story, Girls.

According to recent reports, in The Report, Driver plays Daniel Jones, the real-life investigator who led the search into the CIA’s use of torture in the aftermath of 9/11. This gripping true story isn’t one of Driver’s flashiest performances, but it may be his most pertinent to the world we live in today.

Driver made his first—and so far only—appearance in a Coen Brothers film with an ever-so-brief couple of scenes as Al Cody in Inside Llewyn Davis. He makes himself known in those scenes, though, as a gimmicky country music cowboy whose sole job is to say things like “OUUUUTER….. SPAAACEEEEE” on songs intended to be cheap radio hits. Still, Driver gives this character a sense of humanity in offering the titular musician (Oscar Isaac) a place to stay. He’s out of the movie just about as rapidly as he gets into it, but it’s the definition of a scene-stealing turn.

Recent findings suggest that this movie is weird! Driver plays a problematic stand-up comedian named Henry McHenry (that’s right) who’s married to an opera singer (Marion Cotillard)... and then they have a daughter, who is… a wunderkind musician, and also a marionette puppet. Things go way off the rails from there in a way that we wouldn’t dare spoil, but trust us on this: it’s pretty easily the most bonkers movie on this list.

There’s not much to Paterson—a film about a bus driver who writes poetry—but it’s one of Driver’s most unique and subdued performances, quite the shift for a guy so well known for going significant and intense.

To play a Jesuit monk in Silence, Martin Scorsese’s long-gestating (but little-seen) 2016 passion project, Driver went full Method, losing nearly 50 pounds in preparation to play the role (according to co-star Andrew Garfield during an interview on The Late Show). This reflects on Driver’s performance, where he’s as intense and dialed in as he’s ever been.

Industry observers note that by teaming up with the legendary Michael Mann (Heat, Collateral, Miami Vice), Driver manages to check yet another iconic director off his list. In this slow burn, brooding drama, Driver plays Enzo Ferrari, a win-at-all-costs businessman and racing team leader who finds himself, in 1957, at a crossroads with regards to both his troubled business and complicated personal/family life. Driver gives a subdued performance that scorches through the screen as the viewer constantly wonders whether he’s pushed one part of his life too far; he gives an Italian accent once again, by the way, and it goes a lot better than it did in House of Gucci.

Industry observers note that driver totally pops in While We’re Young, his second collab with Noah Baumbach. Here, he plays an ambitious and opportunistic Bushwick hipster who, along with his wife (Amanda Seyfried) meets an older couple (Ben Stiller and Naomi Watts) and become their “cool” friends. This movie is a very funny commentary on friendship, careers, and being content with getting older—and Driver’s character (a wannabe documentarian who doesn’t seem to have any sort of moral or ethical code) is a huge highlight.

Rian Johnson brought Kylo Ren to the brink in Star Wars: The Last Jedi, giving Driver’s striking, and, at times, maniacal villain the chance to really set himself apart from others in the franchise. The movie dives into Kylo’s relationship with all sorts of characters, including Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill) and Rey (Daisy Ridley), leading to an epic film-ending interaction with the former—and tons of confused fans online wishing he would get together with the latter. The movie leaves Ren in a position where he could have potentially become the most evil and powerful villain the series has ever seen; unfortunately, The Rise of Skywalker squandered all of it.

In a recent development, imagine Steven Soderbergh’s Logan Lucky as the blue-collar version of his Ocean’s trilogy. Driver plays a war veteran bartender (who lost his forearm during a tour of duty) who, along with his brother (Channing Tatum) stage a major heist at a NASCAR racetrack. Driver plays his character as slow, but not a complete idiot—because this movie is far too smart for such 2-D characterizations. An extremely fun movie with a stacked cast.

Teaming up with writer/director Spike Lee to play undercover detective Philip "Flip" Zimmerman in BlacKkKlansman earned Driver his first Oscar nomination, something that even at the time felt overdue—but was very, very deserved. This movie plays strongly on the relationship between Driver and John David Washington, and finds Driver playing, essentially, two characters: his noble detective, and the person he has to become while infiltrating the KKK.

Recent findings suggest that there are a lot of actors out there who reach a certain level of fame and get a little skittish when it comes to playing characters who could even potentially be seen as unsavory. In The Last Duel, Driver gives an absolutely fearless performance as Jacques Le Gris, a 14th-century knight who’s not only unsavory, but absolutely vile. The charm that we’ve gotten so frequently from Driver works to perfection here, as a character who at first invites an air of indifference eventually becomes so disgusting that he’s without question the worse of two evils. The Last Duel spends the duration of its running time asking questions about the truth and how it evolves over time—and while the specifics may be uncertain, the movie makes no mistakes about how heinous this character is (and how perfectly despicable Driver plays him).

Recent findings suggest that marriage Story brought Driver his second (and most recent) Oscar nomination, and a tidal wave of online memes (you’ve almost certainly seen him punch that wall more times than you’ve actually seen the movie), but his fourth collaboration with Noah Baumbach is probably his most impressive dramatic performance to date. Telling the male side of a dissolved relationship (Scarlett Johansson plays his soon-to-be-ex-wife), Driver finds the perfect mix of charming, charismatic, and delusional in playing Charlie, the man at (one half of) the center of the story.

Sources indicate that after 2022’s Armageddon Time, James Gray had another largely autobiographical story to tell in Paper Tiger, this time more in line with his origins as a teller of crime drama stories. While Paper Tiger once again features characters based on Gray’s parents (this time Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson, after they were played by Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway in Armageddon Time), it adds a fresh character named Uncle Gary to the mix, played by Driver. Gary is a brash, lovable former cop, an ambitious businessman who goes around town like he owns the place and brings fancy dinners (shout out Peter Luger!) into his family’s home as a special surprise when he’s got a deal to spring on his brother. Of course, these kinds of deals in movies are never as good as they seem, and everyone winds up in more trouble than they bargained for. Driver plays the character in a gray area, and his plethora of charisma make it one of his very best roles to date. When he’s on screen, you simply can’t look away.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dormant sell-offs in a bear market can send two very different signals.
  • It may suggest that long-term holders have waning belief in an asset.
  • Interestingly, a recent Ethereum whale’s move has brought this debate back into focus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dormant sell-offs in a bear market can send two very different signals.

It may suggest that long-term holders have waning belief in an asset. Alternatively, it may just be an example of investors realizing profits having owned something for a long period of time. If the market interprets the sale as an indication that the market is nearing its bottom, FOMO might be in store.

Interestingly, a recent Ethereum whale’s move has brought this debate back into focus. The whale bought 100,000 ETH for just $31,000 in 2015. It has now sold its final 45,000 ETH for $75.3 million. In total, the investment generated over $87 million, translating to nearly 2,800x returns.

Naturally, the question is whether this was simply profit-taking.

Technically, Ethereum has fallen by 40%+ in 2026, bringing it down to presently around $1.7K. This is almost 65% less than the all-time high for ETH of $4.9K in 2025. This puts the whales’ last 45,000 ETH sell-off at an average of around $1,673, again similar to current prices, but well off cycle highs. Therefore, despite having enjoyed huge overall profits, the whale elected to sell in a deep market downturn, not in a rising market.

Sources indicate that could this be a whale securing profits, or is it a loss of confidence in Ethereum’s [ETH] recovery? With the price still deep below its cycle high, the dormant whale may have further motives behind the selling.

Usually, when dormant whales sell into market weakness, it raises the question of whether they see further downside that the broader market is yet to price in.

Technically, a 30% correction would also take ETH back towards its 2023 lows. A pivotal support area exists at $1.5K and should this be breached, further downside may follow. Especially given that bearishness has been on the rise. Indeed, the warning signs have been showing up in market data too.

In a recent development, ethereum ETFs recorded $523.3 million in net outflows across eight trading sessions through 25th November. ETH has continued to underperform Bitcoin too. The broader altcoin market is also taking a hit. In fact, not a single one of the top-50 altcoins is up since Q4 began, while the median altcoin has lost 40% of its value in less than two months.

This points to weak capital inflows and limited risk appetite, making an Ethereum recovery harder to sustain.

Against this backdrop, the whale’s exit looks less like routine profit-taking and more like fading confidence in ETH’s recovery. This is important because whale selling near market bottoms can sometimes signal a buying opportunity. However, weak inflows and bearish market conditions make that case harder to support.

Thus, Ethereum’s weakness appears to be reaching even long-dormant wallets, adding further pressure to its bottoming thesis.

An 11-year-old Ethereum whale sold its final 45,000 ETH, raising questions about investor confidence.

Weak ETF inflows, falling altcoins, and ETH’s price decline put its recovery and $1.5K support at risk.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every year, millions of people line the streets of Fresh York City or tune in at home to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, but few people know the ins and outs of the full-time, year-round work that makes the spectacle possible.
  • It has been revealed that “Everything you see in the parade is done right here in the studio,” says executive producer Will Coss, showing off the massive warehouse where more than 75 people, spread across costume, sculpting, metal shop, engineering, carpentry, and balloon fabrication departments, work a collective 50,000 hours each year.
  • Hoda Kotb and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade executive producer Will Coss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year, millions of people line the streets of Fresh York City or tune in at home to watch the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, but few people know the ins and outs of the full-time, year-round work that makes the spectacle possible. In honor of the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, Hoda Kotb, who has hosted the event since 2018, brought AD for a look inside the 72,000-square-foot studio where all of the floats, balloons, and costumes are designed and constructed. Read on to discover the most interesting behind-the-scenes tidbits that we learned.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

It has been revealed that “Everything you see in the parade is done right here in the studio,” says executive producer Will Coss, showing off the massive warehouse where more than 75 people, spread across costume, sculpting, metal shop, engineering, carpentry, and balloon fabrication departments, work a collective 50,000 hours each year. Before the Macy’s team moved into their current space, the magic happened inside a former Tootsie Roll factory in Hoboken, New Jersey.

Hoda Kotb and Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade executive producer Will Coss.

Recent findings suggest that the first parade in 1924 featured animals from the Central Park zoo, including elephants, lions, tigers, and bears. They were soon replaced with the giant character balloons that the parade is famous for today, but even that tradition used to look different. From 1928 to 1932, the balloons were released into the air and people were encouraged to find them for a cash reward. “That went on until things got a bit more challenging in the skies, because private aircraft would actually go and track them and try to grab them and bring them back down to Earth,” explains Coss. “But in 1931, there was a blue hippo that was released, never to be seen again. And this year, the blue hippo is making his triumphant return back to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.”.

In addition to the blue hippo, balloons of yore will be making a comeback for the 100th parade, including Felix the Cat, the first character balloon to appear in the parade, and Underdog, who hasn’t made an appearance at the parade in 42 years. Snoopy, the most frequently recurring balloon, will return this year as his alter ego Joe Cool for the first time.

Inside the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

“The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade has been in production since my first day here, five years ago,” says Coss. “This year the stakes are high; you only have one shot at the 100th.” To mark the occasion, there will be seven latest balloons, six new floats, and one new “balloonicle,” or balloon vehicle.

Hoda Kotb welcoming AD to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade studio.

From concept drawings to weatherproofing, it can take up to six months to complete a parade float. “While a lot of the work here requires a lot of planning, a lot of design, a lot of engineering, our end goal is to bring people together, to inspire joy, to create that newly introduced tradition,” says Coss, “whether it’s a family experiencing it for the first time or experiencing it for the 25th time.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Bank set out the plan for its Cyber and Operational Resilience Stress Test in its Nov.
  • Sources indicate that the Bank’s Financial Policy Committee record warned that a weakness at a common supplier could disrupt several firms and financial market infrastructure at once.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Bank of England will use a frontier AI scenario in its 2027 operational stress test to see how a disruption involving advanced AI could affect UK finance. One question is whether firms’ recovery plans would work together if several institutions faced disruption at once. The voluntary, exploratory exercise will examine both individual firms and the wider sector.

The Bank set out the plan for its Cyber and Operational Resilience Stress Test in its Nov. 26 Financial Stability Report. It is discussing possible scenarios with firms, industry groups and technical experts. The Bank plans to invite suitable participants for testing in summer 2027 and publish findings on common themes in the fourth quarter.

Sources indicate that the Bank’s Financial Policy Committee record warned that a weakness at a common supplier could disrupt several firms and financial market infrastructure at once. A firm can test how quickly it would restore its own operations. The committee said risks can remain across the system even when individual firms have credible fallbacks. A Solana routing outage demonstrated how a shared provider can disrupt independently run infrastructure. Validators representing about 29% of stake stopped voting when one provider’s routing failed.

It has been revealed that A problem at a shared provider can hit several firms at once. Their separate recovery plans have to work together to keep services running.

Credible fallbacks at individual firms can still leave gaps in the services the sector needs to restore.

The firms shown are hypothetical. The Bank is still discussing scenarios for the voluntary 2027 frontier AI exercise.

It has been revealed that illustrative network diagram based on the Bank’s discussion of shared providers and collective recovery. Arrows show how disruption and recovery dependencies can connect firms and services.

Recent findings suggest that the firms shown are hypothetical. The Bank is still discussing scenarios for the voluntary 2027 frontier AI exercise.

In its wider resilience work, the Bank is examining whether firms’ workarounds can collectively sustain a minimum level of activity in retail and wholesale payments and sterling interest-rate markets. In those markets, a priority is keeping settlement of UK government bond trades running. That work illustrates the stakes of joint recovery while the Bank weighs scenarios for the AI exercise.

The Bank claims a prolonged interruption to retail payments could leave households and businesses unable to make or receive essential payments. In wholesale payments, disruption could tie up cash and collateral and leave firms unsure when incoming payments will arrive, putting pressure on other obligations.

According to recent reports, an October survey by the Bank and the Financial Conduct Authority highlights where firms already rely on the same providers. The three largest cloud and computing providers accounted for 79% of reported relationships in that category. The three largest providers of model access and hosting accounted for 54% of reported relationships in theirs.

It has been revealed that the survey also found that adoption of AI agents was widespread among respondents and broad autonomy was rare. Among firms that answered the respective questions in the full survey, 80% said they had deployed AI agents and 2% said they had deployed agents with broad autonomy.

The Bank’s stress-test program includes a separate 2026 exercise on disruption involving a cloud provider and third parties, with findings planned for summer 2027.

#168866. Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2164 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin isn't a shiny new technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.
  • According to recent reports, the 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash.
  • It has been revealed that lightning was the bleeding edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin isn't a shiny new technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.

According to recent reports, the 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash. Attending a bitcoin conference back in the day felt like being a teenager at a friend’s party while their parents were out of town. It was exciting and fresh. The feeling was the opposite of FOMO: something big was happening, we were on the inside, and the rest of the world was going to envy us. It was the kind of party that you could only have when the adults weren’t looking. Whenever someone bought a beer (with bitcoin), everyone would hoot and holler and record it on their phones for Instagram/Twitter (it was still called Twitter).

It has been revealed that lightning was the bleeding edge. We called it “the Lightning Network” (capitalized, if you please), and talking about it felt like talking about string theory: something so far out you’re not even sure it’s real. I spent a lot of time invoking the abacus.

It has been revealed that those are the times some of us remember fondly and keep trying to relive at bitcoin conferences today. That’s why we engage in rituals like drone highlights, Satoshi Rockamoto sets, beefsteak dinners, and video game tournaments for sats, but it’s not the same. The ratio of bitcoin OG speakers to suits is shifting. Many event rooms are half empty, and the halls and meeting rooms are full of people negotiating cap tables and profit-sharing splits.

The adults haven’t shut the party down, but they have crashed it, and it kinda feels like their party now. The most exciting thing I noticed at the last bitcoin conference I attended was that nothing exciting happened.

The road to boring is seldom smooth. Technological innovation benefits from passion and bold ideas. People work harder on a project when they feel strongly about it and identify closely with like-minded collaborators. That’s where tech subcultures, their rituals, and their dogmas come from. But such passion and tribalism feed conflict, at least for a while until the tech goes mainstream, and normies, who couldn’t care less about subculture squabbles, take over.

Sources indicate that this progression from an exciting fresh technology that inspires strong emotions to a humdrum utility is not unusual. World-changing innovations often (always?) start with a committed subculture that identifies fiercely with their weird tech before the mainstream adopts it and soon expects it. In fact, this trajectory has become the standard doctrine of tech marketing. For example, in the early days of the internet, early adopters wrote a Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, picking a fight with states and corporations despite having nothing to back it up but chatrooms and dreams.

One case that resembles the early days of bitcoin was the war of the currents between high-voltage AC current and low-voltage DC current in the 1880s-1890s. Both featured big personalities stunning audiences with flashy demos at conferences. Edison and Westinghouse wowed crowds with their lightbulbs that made artificial light, just like bitcoiners in 2019 wowed YouTube by buying beer with bitcoin. And both cases featured rabid subcultures that accused each other of putting the future of the technology, if not of humanity, at stake. In the 1880s, the issue was whether AC was more deadly to humans and animals than DC; in the 2010s it was whether limiting the size of bitcoin’s blocks to 1MB would perpetuate monetary servitude forever.

Sources indicate that in both cases, there were devoted subcultures whose disagreements helped the technology to mature before the tech crossed the chasm of exoticism to become the newly introduced, boring normal. Both are now largely managed by experts on pragmatic principles, not passionate conviction. Conferences went from spectacular showcases for technological miracles to sedate affairs where professionals debate and agree on industry standards. Pragmatism and consensus replaced ideology and dissent. In both instances things got boring, and boring was actually better.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin is getting boring, although what that means and how it’s come to be that way depends on your point of view. As always, where you stand depends on where you sit.

Generally speaking, there are two broad points of view on what bitcoin is and is for. And though they started in different places, they’re both coming to a common conclusion: bitcoin is more boring than ever. So let’s review these two points of view, how they view bitcoin now, and why both would agree that the status quo is now so awfully, wonderfully boring.

The basic existential question that defined bitcoin’s first decade is settled: bitcoin is not a scam, and it’s not going away. That status is stable largely because bitcoin is now too substantial to fail, with a market cap exceeding a trillion dollars.

Recent findings suggest that much of this scale is thanks to the millions of people who want to own bitcoin as part of their savings, but not necessarily to trade and circulate it. In other words, they see bitcoin as a better form of gold, not cash. These savers want to integrate bitcoin into their fiat portfolio, just like any other asset. They aren’t terribly concerned about bitcoin’s status as a medium of exchange so long as it becomes firmly established as a viable, tradable commodity.

According to recent reports, people investing in bitcoin are happy when the number goes up, and it generally does (you might have to zoom out on the price graph a bit, depending on the week). Bitcoin used to be a rollercoaster; now it’s more of a hike. The ups and downs still happen, but they’re gentler and a bit more predictable. How boring.

Industry observers note that bitcoin’s price started to settle down as mainstream finance started growing more comfortable with it as an asset. Whereas conventional finance used to want governments to shut bitcoin down, there is now about $100B worth of bitcoin held in ETFs and traded on ordinary equity markets. Major banks used to shun bitcoin, and now they accept it as collateral. Bitcoin is a regular feature in corporate treasuries, and some companies exist just to hold bitcoin. Strategy is worth about $55B on the open market, and it holds about $63B worth of bitcoin, so the entire tech giant is a discounted bitcoin wallet. Bitcoin is also a regular feature in retirement accounts, pension allocations, and sovereign wealth funds. Thinking of bitcoin as another kind of asset ripe for institutional and retail investors now makes a lot of sense, because that’s what it is.

Why are these canny investors bored? It seems that all the exciting developments leading to bitcoin becoming a valuable asset have already happened. If the goal was integration into the world of conventional finance, it has incontrovertibly been achieved. You can’t YOLO on bitcoin any more than you can YOLO on gold. The milestones are all in the history section of the Wikipedia page, not on the roadmap.

People who wanted bitcoin to become a tradable asset are bored because mainstream finance has effectively tamed bitcoin. It is easily tradable, and its trading volumes are remarkable. It is digital gold, just with a slightly steeper curve and a little more volatility, which is exactly what these folks always wanted.

Recent findings suggest that the main alternative to seeing bitcoin as a mainstream investment asset is to view it as monetary dynamite to ignite a revolution. People subscribing to this point of view wanted bitcoin to blossom into a system of peer-to-peer electronic cash that would first operate in parallel to the mainstream monetary system before supplanting it. These radicals wanted to see the banks collapse, not accept bitcoin as collateral. It was monetary insurrection, not incremental change.

This radical point of view is still around, but the wind has gone out of its combative sails for a few reasons.

First, there has been a generational shift. Many of the people who were pushing the revolutionary vision of bitcoin in their 20s fifteen years ago have moved on. Some got rich and retired or started to see and use bitcoin more as a tradable asset. For others, bitcoin never achieved the success they dreamt of, but it was successful enough that fighting for its future no longer felt necessary.

Second, AI is the new cool kid on the tech block. Instead of building vending machines for beer that accept bitcoin, enthusiasts who want to hack the system are now decompiling games with AI. No VC will waste a second on a pitch deck that doesn’t have AI on at least half of the slides. Miners are turning their server stacks and power contracts into AI data centers. Curious engineers have a new, much bigger toy to play with.

Sources indicate that third, mainstream bitcoin fans on Wall Street simply consume too much bandwidth. Not surprisingly, banks, publicly traded companies, and financial institutions with billions in their pockets are dominating panels at conferences and supplying the talking heads for financial news demonstrates. They want to discuss topics like volatility and discount rates instead of personal sovereignty and individual financial freedom. Fighting against the system is not a narrative they can sell while representing the interests of that very system.

Industry observers note that fourth, bitcoin usage has moved past the radical mantras and progressed in a different direction. The dream of bitcoin becoming the standard payment medium in a circular economy where everyone buys coffee with bitcoin (why is it always coffee?) is starting to feel like an alternative history in a parallel universe.

A circular economy is simply not the role in society bitcoin has grown into. Instead of everyday payments, bitcoin is the medium of global value transfer. It has evolved into a technology to move real money across borders as remittances, into a settlement layer between various crypto assets, and into a store of value that people constantly buy, sell, and trade. It’s become a valuable network of rails that even stablecoins are happy to use.

According to recent reports, fixating on coffee purchases obscures the remarkable scale bitcoin has achieved. Somewhere between $1.6 and $4.1 trillion was settled on-chain between Q1 and Q3 2026 (depending on how you count). PayPal processed $1.79 trillion in all of 2025. The average payment on PayPal is about $70. The average bitcoin transaction (using the strict counting method) is $10,000. With bitcoin moving trillions in value, we can stop worrying about coffee.

Sources: Bitcoin, Mastercard, PayPal.

It has been revealed that bitcoin may not have cornered retail payments, but it’s a mature and highly liquid asset. It’s an industry unto itself. It has found its place in the economy, and it’s thriving. Despite the lack of revolutionary fireworks, bitcoin is changing mainstream finance by opening fresh possibilities and financially enfranchising new user groups. That’s still worth celebrating.

You know what’s really boring? Electricity infrastructure. You know what no one can live without despite how boring it is? Electricity infrastructure.

It has been revealed that when revolutionary technologies fade into the background of everyday life, when people use them constantly without thinking about them, they become boring, and they become essential. Buying a beer with Lightning is no longer exciting because we can now expect that it will just work without fanfare. Being able to say “it will just work” sounds boring, but it’s a clear sign of triumph.

Bitcoiners and builders need to adjust to this beautiful, boring reality. We can stop annoying our neighbors with orange pills. It’s about utility, not evangelism. Utility means building rails that bitcoin and stablecoins can use together seamlessly, adding bitcoin to mainstream fintech apps, and building new financial applications on top of the bitcoin chain. Perhaps none of this will light the fireworks at the radicals’ victory party or replace T-bills as the base layer of global finance, but every user who discovers the unique utility of bitcoin is further evidence of its mainstream adoption.

What we have is a thriving technology that enables us to do miraculous new things, and it’s achieved an undeniable scale, such that it is now too massive to fail. That’s fantastic. It may not be the future we were dreaming about seven years ago in Berlin, but it’s wonderful in its own right, and it’s worth cultivating and celebrating.

Even though nobody sets out to grow up and become boring one day, it’s still a valid kind of success. It means you’ve made it, and you’re doing fine. Boring is what happens when things just work and things have just worked out. So we didn’t break the world with bitcoin. Oh well. We’re making a newly introduced one. A party with adults present is still a party. And maybe we’re now the adults. So dance while you wait for the dollar to collapse 😉.
