Raving in Your 40s, 50s, and 60s? These Women Say It’s the Best Self-Care They’ve Found

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning.
  • In a recent development, that’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo.
  • Midlife women are prioritizing their mental health now more than ever, according to a 2026 study in the journal Women’s Health that analyzed nearly 1,000 surveys about women’s health priorities and concerns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ask Karen Manson, 65, how she likes to recharge, and she’ll tell you this: a night of pounding bass, a sweaty dance floor, and getting home in the wee hours of the morning. She’s loved music her whole life and was always drawn to EDM, but marrying and having kids young left little room to explore it. Then, three years ago, her husband died, and she began thinking about how short and precious life is—and decided it was time to push herself to try new experiences.

In a recent development, that’s how she ended up at her first rave last year, solo. She was nervous, but spent the night dancing, and left with upcoming friends and a newfound confidence. “I felt uninhibited,” she states. She’s attended more than 20 raves since.

Manson isn’t an outlier. Midlife women are prioritizing their mental health now more than ever, according to a 2026 study in the journal Women’s Health that analyzed nearly 1,000 surveys about women’s health priorities and concerns. And a number of them are finding relief on the dance floor.

Industry observers note that A 2025 study in Psychology of Music surveyed 136 women ages 40 to 65 about why they’re involved in EDM experiences. The overwhelming response was that raving was a meaningful part of their mental well-being—an outlet for stress, a source of connection, and a rare place to escape the demands of everyday life, according to the survey.

According to recent reports, “There is a rise in older people attending electronic dance music events, raves, clubs, parties, festivals,” says Alice O’Grady, PhD, a professor of applied performance at the University of Leeds, who co-authored the Psychology of Music study. “The motivations for women going are pretty much characterized as the same as they are for any age: the love of the music, the ability to socialize with existing friends, the atmosphere of the environment, and the sense of community.” Put simply: These music events are plain fun.

The EDM scene is no longer the epitome of youth culture, O’Grady adds, and it’s become more socially acceptable for women to embrace this genre of joy as they get older. That shift may reflect changing attitudes about aging, with women potentially feeling less constrained by traditional expectations about how they’re “supposed” to spend their time as they age. Social media has also made it much easier to discover niche music scenes, while a growing focus on mental health, movement, pleasure, and community may be encouraging women to seek out experiences that just make them feel good.

The older you get, the harder it can be to find a place where you can be playful, spontaneous, and fully present with other people. For some, the rave scene provides exactly that. “You've got more responsibility, more commitments,” O’Grady claims. “You want that escape, you want that ability to connect through music and immerse yourself in an environment that allows you to be expressive and just shake off some of those roles that older women carry.”.

In a recent development, samantha Hillery, 43, started raving in her 20s as a way to let loose and have fun. But as life got busier with work, family, and kids, she stopped going. Years later, while searching for fun things to do in her area with friends, she came across Bingo Loco, a high-energy party with EDM, dancing, confetti, and—yes—bingo, and found her way back to it.

Recent findings suggest that now, Hillery gives herself permission to step away from the endless list of adult responsibilities. “As we get older and super busy with our lives, we forget how fun we maybe used to be, and it seems like something that was so far in the past,” she notes. “But when you’re able to go out and rave surrounded by a bunch of friends and people that just want to have a good time, you remember that part of you isn’t lost.”.

For some, keeping up with friends also becomes more challenging as you age and enter new eras of your life. Social obligations often come second, competing with work schedules, children, relationships, and other obligations, says Madison Liddle, LMHC, a licensed psychotherapist at Madison Liddle Therapy and co-founder of The Practice Co, a co-working space for therapists. At a music event like these, though, spontaneous connection is built into the experience.

Recent findings suggest that hundreds or thousands are gathered around the same music, moving to the same rhythm, creating an immediate sense of belonging. It’s a concept called collective effervescence, which is “a feeling of joy and connection when a group of people are in a shared space doing a shared thing,” Liddle explains. “Social connection is a really strong determinant of health as we age, and raving offers an opportunity to create and be in community with people with shared interests.”.

Recent findings suggest that getting out and meeting new people is the main reason Manson is so attracted to rave culture—she’s found the crowds to be welcoming and friendly. “Life can become quite small if you don't push yourself,” she says, alluding to feeling alone after her husband’s passing. “I enjoy meeting people, I enjoy conversations. I'm not good at home in my own firm—I need socialization.” Dancing with new friends is the way to do that, and it keeps her feeling energized.

Sources indicate that in fact, in Manson’s experience, the EDM scene has seemed remarkably friendly to people of all ages and backgrounds. O’Grady agrees: “Women need spaces that are inclusive, welcoming, and accessible, and the rave scene actually does that quite well,” says O’Grady. You’ll feel a sense of belonging, like you’re part of something bigger than yourself, even if you’re there alone, she adds. The music creates an instant common language, while dancing alongside friends and strangers turns what could be an individual activity into something meaningful and collective.

The physical perks of dancing are well documented. It strengthens the cardiovascular, metabolic, musculoskeletal, and cognitive systems, as WH previously reported. It can also improve coordination, balance, and stability, which becomes especially vital with age. But it can boost your mental health too, mainly because it helps you stay present. When you’re fully focused on what you’re hearing, feeling, and doing, there’s less room to get caught up in the mental replaying and worrying that can fuel stress, Liddle claims.

In fact, many participants in the Psychology of Music study described dancing at raves as a way to ease anxiety, depression, and low moods, claims co-author Alinka Greasley, PhD, a professor of music psychology at the University of Leeds. Anxiety can keep the mind focused on what might go wrong, while depression can make the present feel flat.

According to recent reports, raving, by contrast, demands attention in a different way. Instead of sitting with your thoughts, you’re listening to loud, immersive music, dancing to the beat, and anticipating the next drop, Liddle explains. That physical engagement helps interrupt rumination and creates a sense of clarity that lasts beyond the dance floor; it can help clear your head.

It has been revealed that alex Daly attended her first EDM show at 40 after her partner, who’d been going to raves for years, encouraged her to come along. A year later, raving has become a central part of her wellness routine. If she’s having a stressful week and doesn’t have an EDM show on her calendar, she immediately starts looking for one. “Once I’m in the crowd, I get into a flow state, and moving my body to the beat really helps me process my emotions,” claims Daly, now 41. “Dancing helps me stop ruminating, get out of my head, and back into my body.” For a few hours, there’s simply less room for the mental noise of everyday life. In a way, it’s like the pounding beat is a reset button you can dance to.

Industry observers note that of course, rave culture has long been tied to recreational drugs like MDMA, which can bring on feelings of euphoria, connection, and stress relief. That link hasn’t disappeared. Some of the women in the Psychology of Music study stated they took drugs, often to keep their energy up for dancing, while others went purely for the music and the movement.

It has been revealed that however, drugs weren’t what gave the women a sense of belonging, the study uncovered. “That's very much already there from their perspective,” Greasley says. “The drugs are more to do with [increasing] energy levels and also the marrying of the drugs and the music. Many women called it a spiritual experience to be in ecstatic states whilst dancing to the music.”.

Recent findings suggest that karen D., 62, who asked that her last name be withheld because she discusses her drug use, sees it the same way. She started going to raves in her early 50s with her second husband. While she partakes in recreational drug use, she also knows people who attend raves completely sober. For her, the bonding comes from dancing with like-minded people who are all just happy to be there.

Sources indicate that but Karen acknowledges that drugs heighten those feelings and add to the mental health boost she gets from raving. “I feel like my brain’s reconnecting in ways that it has forgotten how to connect,” she says. “I can get down with what’s going on in my life at times, and it completely transforms me into a much more positive person.”.

Wellness advice in your 40s, 50s, and beyond is often the same advice over and over: protect your sleep, drink less, manage stress, and stick to a routine. But in contrast, this group of ravers finds genuine self-care in the act of staying out late, dancing for hours, and disrupting those prescribed wellness rules. “In this world where everything is so optimized and planned and scheduled, there is something that we lose in terms of fun,” indicates Liddle, noting that raving brings it to the forefront. The key is to accept the occasional trade-off—less sleep in the name of mental health benefits—and to strike a balance between partying and recovering.

According to recent reports, manson has attended a couple of Daybreaker events, which are morning, sober parties and raves, often starting around 6 a.m. Early parties like these are becoming more common. O’Grady adds that more women DJs are putting on earlier demonstrates with the attitude of: “We all want to get together, we all want to have a dance, but we want to be in bed by midnight.”.

However, Manson prefers later highlights because she finds that’s when more traditional EDM is played. But staying up until 4 a.m. at these events has been a bit of a learning curve, so she tries to limit her events to one per weekend. “The enthusiasm's there, but I'm not prepared to spend so much time recovering,” she says. “Once is great, it does what I want it to do. It makes me feel good. I get to connect with people that I enjoy spending time with.” She prioritizes sleeping in the next morning, and just rests the next day if she needs to. Then, she can still go to the gym and take long walks during the week. (She doesn’t work anymore, so she has more flexibility to rest.).

Despite the missed-out-on sleep, Karen D. finds that rave life rejuvenates her. “If I've been away at a festival for a weekend, I come back very tired because I need more sleep,” she says. “However, I do feel refreshed somehow—more clearheaded.”.

It has been revealed that but she still makes sure to still get seven hours of sleep if she goes to bed late, so then she can still fulfill her responsibilities at home, like taking her grandson to school. The tradeoff is also worth it for her, and in fact, going to raves inadvertently benefits her wellness routine. It “really helps motivate me to do weight training, to go running, to do all these wholesome recognized exercises, because I want to stay well to be able to go and dance [until] 3 o'clock in the morning,” she says.

Rave culture is no longer just for younger people, and women in midlife are soaking in every ounce of fun, freedom, community, and release. “They don't want to be defined by their age, but more importantly, they don't want to be restricted by it,” says O’Grady. “Saying, ‘I want to dress up in my sequins, I want to put my face on, I want to go and have a dance, I want to stay out all night and shrug off my responsibilities for a little while, I want all of that and why shouldn't I?’”.

For Manson, getting ready is part of the appeal, and she’s collected a variety of vibrant, fun outfits to go out in. “It's almost like creating a bit of an identity, which I'm quite enjoying,” she says. At this stage of life, raving has given her a way to reinvent herself.

It has been revealed that midlife can chip away at a woman’s confidence and leave her feeling overlooked. Raving pushes back on that by giving women a place to be bold and seen. As Karen D. puts it, “Women of my age can often disappear or become invisible, and it's almost the opposite of that.”.

Since her husband’s death, Manson has made a point of pushing herself to try fresh things. Raving has given her lasting memories, a fresh outlook, and a crew of friends who aren’t ready to stop dancing anytime soon. “I live with the feeling that life’s very short and precious,” she indicates, “so seize the moment.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we want to let you in on a secret: You can replicate the good night’s rest you get at luxury destinations by dressing your bed with the hotel-quality sheets. Aside from accessories like fluffy down feather pillows and mattress toppers, we often attribute cotton percale and sateen to a five-star sleep.

In a recent development, to get down to the nitty-gritty of these sheets, a hotel bed dressed in a percale weave boasts a crisp look and feel, almost as if it were made from your favorite pressed button-down shirt. A sateen weave, however, is polished and resembles the appearance of pearls. What’s more, both of these high-quality sheets have breathable, wrinkle-resistant qualities for a refined aesthetic we know and love in a high-end establishment.

Many of our favorite places to buy bedding—including Italian luxury brands like Frette—even create custom bed linens like these for the best hotels around the world. Scroll below for a staycation-style set of sheets.

Recent findings suggest that for consistency, all of the prices reflect queen sizes. However, many brands offer twin size and king size options too.

Recent findings suggest that the Andersen Hotel, a family-owned boutique retreat in Copenhagen, offers guests sheets, towels, and robes from the editor-favorite brand Boll & Branch. To mimic the experience at home, you can shop the entire collection, including the Signature Hemmed Sheet Set tested and beloved by contributor Rachel Fletcher. The buttery-soft cotton sateen set is made with long-staple cotton fibers, and only gets softer with each wash. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, makes them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” Fletcher shares. After more than five years with these sheets, Fletcher adds that there are no signs of pilling or wear, “just that coveted softness which feels lived-in but not worn out.”.

It has been revealed that matouk is a legacy brand known for bespoke touches on high-thread-count sheets. Their hotel collection is found in a number of luxury resorts and historic inns, including Hotel Barrière Fouquet's in Latest York City and renowned Arizona wellness escape Castle Hot Springs. The Bergamo is their most lightweight percale sheet, combining Giza 87 and 92 Egyptian cotton yarns. “I hate scratchy sheets, and I breathed a sigh of relief when I slipped into these,” indicates contributor Allie Weiss. “They are lightweight, crisp-looking, and soft to the touch.” We also recommend taking advantage of their personalization feature, which allows you to add a monogram to the edge of the sheet. Just remember that each piece is sold separately, so you’ll have to build your own bedscape.

Recent findings suggest that another property with Frette bedding, The Palace Hotel in Madrid is an AD-favorite historic hotel. “You’ll definitely want to stop by La Cúpula during your trip for an afternoon drink and some bites from the stylish tapas menu,” indicates shopping editor Audrey Lee. “If it’s the right time of day, the room becomes drenched in sunlight through the dome-shaped stained glass ceiling.” As for the bedding, you can mirror the hotel’s lavish interiors with Frette’s bold sheets. The polished sateen set boasts a thick border in six color combinations to wake up a bedroom.

Sources indicate that make a statement without sacrificing a classic hotel look with this tuxedo sheet set. Crafted by Frette for the Ritz-Carlton, this design includes a white-on-white stripe pattern that is perfect for a suite-inspired space. For a unique touch, you can also pair a set of the classic pillowcases with this set for a blend of solid colors and bold lines. Instead of shorter threads that can fray over time, this fabric is made of extra-long staple cotton sateen for an ultra-soft and durable feel.

Priding themselves on a sustainable outlook toward hospitality, the 1 Hotel Group offers a connection with nature and serenity even in the heart of the city. With green-certified buildings and a focus on wellness, it’s no surprise that this hotel’s bedding is equally natural. Kassatex’s 100% cotton sheets are softer than percale but not as shiny as sateen. Contributor Kate McGregor stayed at the 1 Hotel Seattle and was impressed with the breathability. “I’m quite a hot sleeper, but even after a cross-country flight, I slept soundly,” she says. “There was no swishing noise as I moved, either, a pet peeve of mine with really crisp hotel sheets.” Machine washable and available in either a queen or king set, these sheets come with a 60-day trial, so you can really get a feel for them without worrying about a wasted investment.

What Type of Sheets Do Five-Star Hotels Use?

It has been revealed that while it varies from property to property, the majority of the hotels on this list use white cotton sheets. Whether percale or sateen, the best hotel sheets all offer a neat, design-agnostic look that suits the center of New York just as well as the rolling hills of Tuscany. Percale will have an added crispness and cooling factor, while sateen will have an added shine and smoothness. Regardless of material finish, look for an all-natural fiber makeup (like 100% cotton) and a versatile white colorway.

Why Do Hotels Like to Use White Bed Sheets?

From an aesthetic perspective, white sheets offer a cloudlike, serene escape for the guest. They also look the cleanest. Stark white sheets cannot hide stains or wear and tear as darker colors can—you can see exactly where each thread has snagged. White bedding is also the most easily sanitized; it even has its own setting on your washing machine. Bleach is necessary to kill germs, especially in a commercial setting, and you don’t want to risk the color fading and yellow stains that can occur on colored sheets.

What Type of Sheets Does The Ritz-Carlton Use?

Recent findings suggest that the Ritz-Carlton uses white cotton sheets from luxury bedding brand Frette. The extra-long staple cotton is more durable than short strands, proven wash after wash. Boasting a subtle monochromatic stripe, The Ritz-Carlton’s sheets play with texture without departing from the clean lines and opulent energy of their suites' overall design scheme.

What Fabrics Are the Best Sheets Made of?

Long or extra-long-staple cotton sheets are considered the “best,” in our experience. These typically have a smooth finish and hold up well over time. That noted, so much of it comes down to your own personal preferences. “[Deciding] which one is best for a particular person or climate is relative,” Katie Glusica, professor in the fibers department at the Savannah College of Art and Design, previously shared. “A percale in the 200 to 400 thread-count range will be durable and have a cooler sensation and a lighter weight feel, best for people who run a little warm or where the climate is warmer. Sateen sheets in the 300- to 600-thread-count range are best for someone looking for softness over durability, and better for cooler climates where a heavier feeling sheet is more comfortable.” Then, there are the more seasonal fabrics like airy linen for summer or thick flannel for winter. If you’re still undecided, we often find that Goldilocks-level comfort in cotton sheets with thread counts between 200 and 600 threads per inch.

What Are the Best Bed Sheets for Hot Sleepers and Cold Sleepers?

While percale is recommended for hot or warm sleepers, compared to other cotton sheets, shopping writer Julia Harrison argues the best is bamboo or Tencel lyocell. “AD editors and I prefer these natural fibers because they usually feel cool and gentle against skin, but they also have great temperature regulating qualities since the fabric absorbs excess moisture to help you stay refreshed while you sleep,” she says.

And during the winter months, or for those who run cold year-round, there’s nothing more comforting than sinking into a bed dressed in flannel sheets. “These are great for keeping you cozy and toasty because of a brushed (and sometimes double-brushed) cotton material that feels soft to the touch,” says senior shopping editor Nashia Baker. “It depends on the brand, but some make their sheets with 100% long-staple cotton, like supima cotton, that’s known for its durability without wear over time.”.

What Is the Difference Between Percale and Sateen?

Industry observers note that both are made from cotton, but the weave is what differentiates the two. “Percale is a classic one-over, one-under construction that creates a crisp, breathable fabric with a matte finish reminiscent of fine poplin shirting, while sateen’s longer thread float produces a smoother hand and subtle sheen,” Rebecca Weinstein, vice president of design at Highgate, the management organization for the Atlas Hotel in Boston, previously told AD. Hot sleepers will feel most comfortable in cooling sheets like percale, while those who prefer a less structured, smooth feel will likely splurge on sateen. “Sateen is more dense, with more threads packed in, so the fabric is warmer,” shared Preeti Gopinath, associate professor of textiles and founding director of the MFA textiles program at Parsons School of Design in New York. “Percale is cooler, and with a thread count of 150 to 200, there is less fabric per square inch, which allows for better airflow.”.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (639 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Russia’s VTB Opens Bitcoin Trading as Central Bank Finalizes Crypto Test

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian bank VTB began letting brokerage clients buy and sell bitcoin in its investing app on Friday, a day after the Bank of Russia approved the knowledge test every Russian crypto buyer now has to pass.
  • According to recent reports, starting Nov.
  • Sources indicate that “In our model, access to cryptocurrencies will require qualified investor status and passing special testing,” Andrei Yatskov, head of brokerage services at VTB, said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian bank VTB began letting brokerage clients buy and sell bitcoin in its investing app on Friday, a day after the Bank of Russia approved the knowledge test every Russian crypto buyer now has to pass.

According to recent reports, starting Nov. 27, clients of VTB’s brokerage can trade cryptocurrencies in the VTB My Investments app, the broker mentioned. For now, the trades happen over the counter rather than on an exchange, and access is limited to qualified investors, the legal term for Russians who meet wealth or experience thresholds, who also pass the new test.

Sources indicate that “In our model, access to cryptocurrencies will require qualified investor status and passing special testing,” Andrei Yatskov, head of brokerage services at VTB, said. He said the test would appear in the app on Nov. 27 and work like the bank’s existing tests for other instruments.

VTB handles the buying, storage and record-keeping itself on Russian infrastructure. To trade, clients need to open a separate digital account at VTB’s digital depository, where the crypto is held, on top of their regular brokerage account. The bank received its digital depository and crypto exchange licenses on Oct. 6.

“At the start, we will focus on buying and selling cryptocurrencies, and then we will introduce additional services as regulation develops,” Yatskov noted.

In a recent development, the launch came quickly after the regulator moved. On Nov. 26, the Bank of Russia approved the first basic standards for brokers and crypto exchange offices, setting the rules for the test. Every investor has to take it, qualified or not, and it is free.

In a recent development, buyers must answer at least seven of eight questions correctly. The standard lays out eight topic blocks, from regulation, technical basics and information security to stablecoins, low-liquidity coins, address labeling and blocked transactions, and volatility, with one question drawn at random from each.

Investors who fail can try once more the same day, with different questions. Brokers are barred from sharing the correct answers with clients or telling them which questions they missed. A passing result stays valid for one year from the test date or the latest trade, whichever comes later.

Industry observers note that the test was the missing piece for Russian banks. When retail buying became legal on Nov. 17, T-Bank said it was waiting on a market standard for testing, and VTB said it was waiting on the remaining rules. Under the broker standard, the industry’s self-regulatory organization has three working days after publication to send brokers the answer options and correct answers.

According to recent reports, ordinary investors still face tight limits once they pass. Non-qualified buyers can only purchase bitcoin, ether and Tether’s USDT, and no more than 300,000 rubles a year through a single intermediary.

Exchange trading is next. SPB Exchange said Friday it will open spot trading in bitcoin, ether and USDT against the ruble on Dec. 1, after the Bank of Russia added it to the registry of digital depositories on Nov. 27. Trading will run from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Moscow time, with same-day settlement in rubles.

Investors won’t all get in on day one. SPB Exchange said brokers will first use the market to set up their systems, and access will open as each broker is ready. TRX and USDC are also approved, but only for qualified investors, with a start date still to come.

Russian exchanges have been allowed to run organized crypto trading since Nov. 22, once the central bank signs off on their rules. Moscow Exchange has also been aiming to open bitcoin trading on Dec. 1.

“We expect that in 2027, as brokers become ready, investor access to the spot market will expand and fresh products and investment services will appear,” stated Evgeny Serdyukov, SPB Exchange’s chief executive.

#168780. Industry News: Vitamin C May Lower Your Risk of Cancer from Certain Processed Foods

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1043 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Vitamin C May Lower Your Risk of Cancer from Certain Processed Foods

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While diving into a plate of bacon or noshing on some salami is always tasty, there’s been growing concern that compounds found in cured meats may raise the risk of cancer.
  • Now, fresh research published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology suggests a possible solution: Take a carefully timed vitamin C supplement.
  • Sources indicate that researchers stress that this doesn’t mean you should pop a vitamin C every time you have bacon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While diving into a plate of bacon or noshing on some salami is always tasty, there’s been growing concern that compounds found in cured meats may raise the risk of cancer. Specifically, once they hit your stomach, nitrates and nitrites found in these foods can spark a chain reaction called nitrosation that allows carcinogens to develop. This isn’t just a meat-eating glitch either: fruits and vegetables that have grown in areas affected by pollution can also lead to this chain reaction.

Now, fresh research published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology suggests a possible solution: Take a carefully timed vitamin C supplement. It can cut this chain reaction and, in theory, lower the odds that carcinogens will develop after eating certain foods linked to this reaction, according to the findings.

Sources indicate that researchers stress that this doesn’t mean you should pop a vitamin C every time you have bacon. But the findings raise a lot of questions about why this may work and how to actually put it into practice in a safe way. Here’s what the researcher behind the study and dietitians want you to keep in mind.

It has been revealed that meet the experts: Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo; Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers; and Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

Recent findings suggest that for the study, researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body, and where they undergo chemical changes. The model looked at a range of areas, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma (i.e. the liquid part of your blood). Researchers discovered that having vitamin C alongside foods that contain nitrates and nitrites may halt chain reactions that happen in the body, including nitrosation, which makes substances that are linked to cancer development.

Sources indicate that the researchers also looked at whether taking vitamin C after each meal could help, and found that it may reduce the formation of nitrosation products linked with cancer risk. The boost was most meaningful when people had foods that contained nitrates and nitrites, like salami, bacon, and other processed meats.

The researchers also theorized that this may explain why certain types of produce that happen to contain both vitamin C and nitrates (like spinach) don’t seem to increase cancer risk, while others do.

Recent findings suggest that it’s notable to stress this: The study was based on a mathematical model and was not a clinical trial or data analysis. Because of that, it's hard to draw too many conclusions right now.

In a recent development, still, this link isn’t out of nowhere. “Under acidic conditions in the stomach, nitrites can undergo chemical reactions that lead to the formation of potentially harmful N-nitroso compounds,” states Gordon R. McNicol, PhD, lead study author and postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Waterloo. “Vitamin C can interfere with these reactions, reducing the formation of these compounds.”.

Sources indicate that why vitamin C? “Vitamin C is an antioxidant,” points out Jessica Cording, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Little Book of Game-Changers. Meaning, it helps to neutralize unstable molecules in the body—and may do the same for nitrosation.

Recent findings suggest that but the effectiveness of vitamin C depends on when it’s in the stomach compared to when these reactions happen, McNicol adds. “Our simulations suggest that taking vitamin C shortly after meals could be particularly effective, as this allows vitamin C to overlap more closely with periods when nitrosation would otherwise be relatively high,” he says.

Experts stress that it’s crucial to keep the study in perspective. “While the findings are promising, more research is needed to determine whether taking vitamin C after meals actually reduces cancer risk,” states Keri Gans, MS, RD, registered dietitian and author of The Small Change Diet.

It has been revealed that cording agrees, stressing that while the findings are “promising,” they’re still just based on a mathematical model at this point. “That said, getting enough vitamin C and other antioxidants, alongside nutrients like fiber and other beneficial plant compounds, has been associated with reduced risk of disease and with overall immune system function,” Cording says. “There are lots of great reasons to include vitamin-C rich fruits and vegetables throughout the day.”.

According to recent reports, there are other things to consider, like practicality and safety. “Our research does not establish that taking vitamin C supplements after every meal is necessary or advisable,” McNicol says. “Although our simulations suggest that dividing a fixed daily supplement across meals may be more effective than taking the same amount at once, further experimental and clinical studies are needed to determine whether these strategies are effective and safe in people.”.

High doses of vitamin C from supplements can also lead to GI discomfort, including nausea and diarrhea, Gans points out.

For now, this is more of an interesting finding vs. an actual dietary recommendation. “Until we have more research, there's no reason to recommend intentionally adding extra vitamin C, whether from food or supplements, after every meal specifically to reduce cancer risk,” Gans notes.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

According to recent reports, carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

#168776. Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension a Month After $6.3 Billion Hack

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (650 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bitcoinmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Binance Fully Lifts Withdrawal Suspension a Month After $6.3 Billion Hack

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it put in place after last month’s record $6.3 billion hack, saying its recovery work is complete and that withdrawals are open across nearly all networks.
  • According to recent reports, “Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted,” the exchange noted in an X post Thursday afternoon.
  • It has been revealed that the revision closes out a month of phased reopenings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binance has fully lifted the withdrawal suspension it put in place after last month’s record $6.3 billion hack, saying its recovery work is complete and that withdrawals are open across nearly all networks.

According to recent reports, “Our withdrawal recovery work is completed and the withdrawal suspension from the security incident has been fully lifted,” the exchange noted in an X post Thursday afternoon. A small number of networks remain paused for maintenance, which Binance called standard practice and said was unrelated to the hack.

It has been revealed that the revision closes out a month of phased reopenings. Binance confirmed the breach on Oct. 29, saying its initial investigation pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave the attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawals.

Industry observers note that the world’s largest crypto exchange stopped all customer withdrawals for two days after the theft, Reuters reported. When they first reopened, customers pulled a net $4.7 billion off the platform, Binance remarked on Nov. 2.

Binance noted on Nov. 12 that it had completed coverage of the affected assets with more than $6.34 billion of tech giant funds. The money came from a partial draw on its Secure Asset Fund for Owners, part of its futures insurance fund and its corporate treasury, and the exchange pledged to rebuild SAFU to about $1 billion.

Sources indicate that coverage is not the same as recovery. Binance replaced the stolen tokens from its own books, while about $2.85 billion of the stolen funds have been frozen remotely by the companies that matter them. The rest remains in the hands of the attackers.

U.S. authorities have blamed North Korean hackers for the theft, which North Korea denies. On Nov. 23, the Justice Department moved to forfeit more than $1.1 billion in USDC that Circle froze, and noted the U.S. has helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion since the attack.

Sources indicate that the unfrozen funds are on the move. North Korean launderers have stepped up transfers through THORChain and a coinjoin service in recent days, blockchain researchers told Reuters, as part of an operation spanning tens of thousands of transactions across blockchains.

It has been revealed that chainalysis and Elliptic estimate that more than $600 million of the stolen crypto has passed through THORChain, though Elliptic stated that figure could count funds that went through more than once. TRM Labs estimates THORChain earned as much as $1 million in fees from the swaps.

Separately, $342 million has moved through a coinjoin service mostly coordinated by a pseudonymous figure named Kruw, Elliptic remarked. A coinjoin combines coins from many users into a single transaction, so their origin is no longer visible on the blockchain. Elliptic has said the launderers will still need other services, such as over-the-counter brokers, to turn the coins into cash.

It has been revealed that the FBI on Oct. 31 published wallet addresses used by the attacker and asked crypto service providers, including the network of computers that runs THORChain, to block them. In a video posted Thursday, THORChain co-founder Chad Barraford remarked 98% of trading on the network was for people’s “own individual financial freedom and liberty.”.

In a recent development, THORChain, which describes itself as decentralized, indicates on its website that it does not “censor” transactions or run Know-Your-Customer checks. Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs, called the FBI’s move to single out the network’s operators “pretty extraordinary.”.

In a recent development, redbord said the laundering could take months or even years, and that cashing out even a fraction would be a windfall for North Korea. The total stolen from Binance equals about a sixth of the country’s estimated gross domestic product.

“They don’t have to get a lot off in order to make this all worthwhile for them,” Redbord stated.

The playroom was a priority from the first meeting. Beneath the cork and rubber underlayment is half an inch of soundproofing. Build-out by Gefen Builders; padded walls and drapery in Fabricut; pendant by Vakkerlight.

Jade Cargill Was a Basketball Player Before the WWE. Here’s What Changed Everything

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Given the ease with which WWE superstar Jade Cargill delivers a pump kick or spinebuster, it’s hard to believe the 34-year-old hasn’t spent her entire life in the ring.
  • Sources indicate that the experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling.
  • According to recent reports, “I can only be as great as my partner,” she tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Given the ease with which WWE superstar Jade Cargill delivers a pump kick or spinebuster, it’s hard to believe the 34-year-old hasn’t spent her entire life in the ring. But growing up, Jade was obsessed with a different sport: basketball. In college, she was a forward/guard for the Jacksonville University team then went on to play overseas in France.

Sources indicate that the experience of being a team player has come in handy for Jade as she navigates the world of wrestling. Sure, it may often look like a one-on-one competition, but Jade notes that, if anything, it’s more like a dance.

According to recent reports, “I can only be as great as my partner,” she tells editors Abigail Cuffey, Amanda Lucci, and Jacqueline Andriakos on the latest episode of The Huddle. “I can't do this by myself.”.

Industry observers note that despite having been a part of the WWE since 2023, Jade admits she’s still a “rookie” compared to her ‘dance’ partners—the other women in the league, who inspire her every day. “I've been placed in a very amazing environment with women who strive for greatness, and that's what I want to do,” she states.

As she prepares to lead a five-woman team at Survivor Series: WarGames on November 28, Jade talks about her unconventional path to wrestling, making peace with mistakes, and the advice she wants every kid watching her to hear.

It has been revealed that jade’s journey to becoming a professional wrestler is the stuff of motivational sports movies. A stay-at-home mom (she took time off work as a child psychologist to raise her daughter), Jade was simply training in the gym to get strong after pregnancy when she was introduced to WWE veteran Mark Henry, who asked if she’d ever considered a career in wrestling.

“I was like, ‘Why not?’” she recalls thinking. “I had a kid and put my life on hold for a little bit. I wanted to do something more. I was like, ‘This body is not done.’ [I] went to a tryout, had no experience at all.”.

Recent findings suggest that jade left that tryout bruised and battered—and determined to improve. And so she trained and trained and trained some more. She couldn’t get enough. “I just loved it,” she says. “It's athletics, yes, but also it's improvising, but also it's acting, but also it's your natural instinct. It’s all these things wrapped into one that I just didn't want to put down.”.

All that work eventually paid off: Jade made her professional wrestling debut with All Elite Wrestling in 2020 and then joined the WWE three years later.

Despite all the training and preparation that goes into a match, Jade admits that not a single one has been “perfect.” But in the case where she stumbles off the ropes or throws a lousy punch, Jade simply follows the old maxim, the show must go on.

“I just kind of have the mindset that these things happen,” she states. “If you do have a mishap, you can't sell it—[the audience doesn’t] know what's going on. You just got to keep going with the punches.”.

Jade also gives a lot of credit to her fellow competitors, who often pick her up—if not physically, then emotionally—after a match, letting her know she’s not alone.

“I remember my coworker Naomi sent me a clip of her falling, and she was like, ‘Just to show you...’ And I was like, ‘Okay, all right. It happens,’” Jade states. “You’ve just got to keep on going and make your next match the best match.”.

Sources indicate that as a mom, Jade knows how powerful an adult’s example can be—whether it’s a parent’s or a performer’s. Ultimately, she hopes kids are inspired by her hard work and determination, both in and out of the ring, and if they can take away any message, it would be this: “Don't let anyone tell you who you are,” she indicates. “Don't let society put you in a box. Go out there and take on the world.”.

And when a latest opportunity presents itself, don’t be afraid to give it a try. “If you would have told me five years ago, I would be wrestling. I would have laughed,” she states. “And look at me now.”.

To hear more from Jade—including her no-frills recovery program—click play on the latest episode of The Huddle above.

#168760. Latest Update: Why So Many New Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1918 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Why So Many New Moms Are Told to Wait to Exercise Again—and What the Research Really Says

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment.
  • Sources indicate that “I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter indicates.
  • It has been revealed that the problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this year, trainer and WH advisory board member Sohee Carpenter, CSCS, posted an Instagram Reel challenging some conventional postpartum advice: Don’t work out until your ob-gyn clears you at your six-week follow-up appointment. Her point wasn’t that new moms should rush back to the gym. It was that one timeline can’t fit everyone. Some women are ready to move sooner, and others need more time.

The Reel ruffled some feathers.

Sources indicate that “I feel like so many people get angry because they assume we mean you're going to be doing a one-rep max back squat a week after you have a baby,” Carpenter indicates. “But that's definitely not what we're saying.” (By “we,” she means trainers who keep up with the latest research on pregnancy and postpartum exercise.).

It has been revealed that the problem, Carpenter explains, is that the six-week rule isn’t based on evidence. On the contrary, research suggests that this type of blanket advice doesn’t make sense for something as personal as postpartum recovery. When you return to exercise after childbirth should depend on your own symptoms, not a date on the calendar.

Recent findings suggest that “There's really nothing magical about the six-week time point,” says Margie Davenport, PhD, a professor of kinesiology at the University of Alberta and chair of the 2025 Canadian Guidelines for Physical Activity for Pregnancy and Postpartum—the first-ever exercise guidelines to specifically focus on evidence-based suggestions for that first year postpartum. In the U.S., the main guidance from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) covers pregnancy and the postpartum period together. ACOG’s guidance points in the same direction, though: It says many women can start exercising again within days of an uncomplicated birth. In fact, “there is no identified ideal time to return,” Davenport says.

Based on the wide range of comments on Carpenter’s post—some supportive, some hypercritical, and still others asking more questions to try to better understand this shift away from the advice they’ve always heard—there’s still a lot of confusion around postpartum exercise. So we asked experts to break down what the research actually claims, and how to approach working out in this upcoming chapter of life.

In many cultures, the first 30 or 40 days postpartum is traditionally considered a protected time to rest, relax, and recover, Davenport notes. In Chinese culture, it’s called zuo yuezi, which translates to “sitting the month.” In many Latin American and Latino communities, it’s known as “la cuarentena,” a nod to its roughly 40-day length. In South Korea, it’s sanhujori, or “postpartum care.”.

Industry observers note that these traditions carry deep cultural significance and are meant to offer real healing and support after birth from one’s community (they put “it takes a village” into practice). They’re rooted in caregiving and cultural custom, and they were never meant to serve as a medical timeline for when it’s safe to start exercising.

In Western medicine, six weeks has become an vital medical benchmark in postpartum recovery—and, over time, a default point for returning to exercise too. “At that point, your uterus should be back to its pre-pregnancy state, and so a lot of the gynecologic changes should be fairly reversed by that point,” says Rita Deering, DPT, PhD, associate professor of exercise science and director of the Pelvic Health, Exercise & Musculoskeletal (PHEM) Research Laboratory at Marquette University.

The first six weeks after birth are also when the risk of complications like high blood pressure and infection is highest, Deering states, which is part of why that window became an crucial medical checkpoint (even though some pregnancy-related changes take longer to resolve). But, she says, “it was never intended to be about exercise.”.

So how did six weeks become the exercise rule? Before researchers knew much about how safe it is to exercise during pregnancy and after birth, working out was considered potentially risky, Deering states. There wasn’t strong evidence that exercise wouldn’t slow healing or raise the odds of complications. So the most cautious advice was simply to wait until a doctor confirmed you’d healed enough to resume physical activity.

It has been revealed that to come up with the 2025 Canadian Guidelines, researchers did a deep dive of all the available research on the topic, which included 574 unique studies organized into seven systematic reviews based on 21 different outcomes of postpartum exercise—such as depression and anxiety, low-back pain, injuries, glucose and blood pressure levels, and more. They also assembled an international panel of experts to give their recommendations.

It has been revealed that their advice: Start light-intensity physical activity and mobilization (think: carrying your baby around your home, a slow walk down the block, pelvic floor physical therapy) right away. From there, progress as you feel ready to moderate-to-vigorous activity such as brisk walking, resistance training, and running at your own pace—as long as tears and incisions have sufficiently healed and you don’t experience additional bleeding with exercise. (As mentioned, ACOG similarly recommends that women can return to postnatal exercise within days after an uncomplicated birth.).

Sources indicate that based on the research, there are no “absolute contraindications” to exercise postpartum, Davenport says—meaning no condition would rule out exercise entirely. There are some relative contraindications, she explains, “where you might have to delay a little bit or modify the type of activity that you're doing.” Examples include severe abdominal pain, extreme fatigue, and C-section incision pain that worsens with activity. All warrant a conversation with your doctor before starting.

It has been revealed that want to Know More About Lifting While Pregnant? Start Here.

According to recent reports, pelvic floor symptoms, like leaking urine or a feeling of heaviness in the vagina, aren’t a reason to stop exercising altogether. If you notice signs of pelvic floor dysfunction, the guidelines recommend starting slowly and building up gradually instead. “Some leakage is okay,” Davenport claims. “It means that the training that you’re doing is just overloading the muscle.”.

Sources indicate that many people, including plenty of commenters on Carpenter’s Reel, worry that exercising after birth will damage the pelvic floor and cause dysfunction. But the evidence doesn’t support that. In fact, those muscles will likely be better off if you resume training, especially if you do exercises to target them in particular. “Engaging in pelvic floor muscle training reduces your risk of urinary incontinence by around 37 percent,” Davenport states. Additionally, if you stop all exercise because you're leaking a little bit, “this can actually mean that you're missing out on those other benefits.”.

Recent findings suggest that one caveat: If you’re leaking a lot, or it’s getting worse over time, “you probably need to pull it back,” Davenport indicates. That means being more selective about the moves you choose. For example, you might skip long runs and high-impact moves like jump squats for now, adds Sheridan Skye, a registered nurse, pre- and postnatal fitness coach, and founder of The Female Fitness Formula. Stick with lower-impact exercises, then build up gradually as you get stronger and your symptoms level off or improve.

In a recent development, at the end of the day, every body, birth, and recovery is vastly different. “Some people have a very uncomplicated labor and delivery and pregnancy; for others, it's quite complex,” states Davenport. “It only makes sense that the way that they're returning and what time they're actually returning is also going to be quite individualized.”.

Industry observers note that for some newly introduced moms, six weeks is too soon, and a blanket deadline only adds stress. “Maybe they aren't sleeping or they don't have the support to be able to return [to exercise] at six weeks,” Davenport says. On the flip side, for someone who had a straightforward delivery and is itching to get moving again, “telling them to wait for six weeks with no evidence to support it is also inappropriate.”.

Sources indicate that in fact, exercise can offer significant benefits during postpartum recovery, even before the six-week mark. “It improves muscle and bone density that we lose throughout pregnancy,” Skye indicates. Postpartum exercise is associated with a 45 percent reduction in the odds of developing postpartum depression, and starting before 12 weeks is even more beneficial.

It’s also associated with a 28 percent reduction in the risk of developing diabetes postpartum. Exercise even improves sleep quality, Skye notes. “Women tend to feel more energized and like they've experienced more rest, even if they haven't,” she says. (Anyone who’s survived a 3 a.m. feeding stretch knows that’s no small thing!).

Recent findings suggest that there is also evidence that exercise in general can help to decrease pain, claims Deering, and research links sedentary behavior to lumbopelvic (the areas of the lower back and pelvis) pain. “So if you are having pain, movement might be what you need to help with that.”.

Sources indicate that for many people, it may be difficult to know if you’re truly ready. “Especially when you're postpartum, it can feel like you are super out of touch with your body sensations, especially if you're not sleeping well,” Carpenter claims.

Sources indicate that if you're at the point where you're thinking about it, but are nervous or unsure or just overwhelmed by having another decision to make, Davenport recommends taking the Get Active Questionnaire for Postpartum—a tool that her team designed as part of the 2025 guideline. It can help you promptly understand if you’re ready to start from a medical perspective. That can help give you some reassurance.

Recent findings suggest that there can also be “a lot of fear involved,” Carpenter indicates, especially if you had a C-section or are healing from a vaginal tear. In that case, “you’re probably going to be a bit hesitant,” which is completely understandable. Starting slower and lighter than you think you need to is perfectly fine as you get reacquainted with your body. “The first several sessions are really about mentally trying to get that confidence back,” she says.

As you go, pay attention to how your body responds. Leaking, for instance? That’s not a reason to stop exercising, but you may want to adjust your workout to reduce it. More bleeding, new pain, or a sense that something just doesn’t feel right are signs to stop, reassess, and possibly scale back. If they don’t improve, check in with your doctor. “It’s really about setting your ego aside and being willing to modify, even if it’s one rep to the next, based on how you’re feeling right at that time,” Carpenter claims.

And if you feel physically ready but aren’t quite there mentally? “It’s okay to honor those feelings,” Deering indicates, “and to recognize that it’s okay to give yourself some time.” Whether that’s two weeks, six weeks, or six months, the right moment to start moving is the one that works for you.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, long ago, in Barcelona, the laundry of the middle-class residents of the Eixample neighborhood was washed in the wells on Calle Aiguafreda, one of the city’s most picturesque streets. Washerwomen and their families lived in narrow, two-story houses, and the women would go to the wells every day to hand-wash clothes. It is in this unique part of the city that you’ll find one of architect Raúl Sánchez’s latest projects.

It has been revealed that the lower entrance to the house and its arbor, on the Calle Aiguafreda side of the building. From here, you can see the living area, a corner of the kitchen island, the bottom of the blue light well, and the white-painted beams. Santina chairs from the 1970s are by Carlo Sant.

“It’s a modest little two-story home on a street that has since lost its original function as a place to wash clothes. We were asked to restore it for a couple and their child,” explains Sánchez. The house faces two streets: Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers. Since there’s a five-foot difference in the elevation of the two streets, Sánchez decided to add a landing at the higher entrance off Granollers, where one flight of stairs descends to a lower level, which opens onto Calle Aiguafreda, and the other ascends to the upper level of the small house, where the bedrooms and a bathroom are located.

In the living room, the floor is made of terra-cotta tiles that echo the traditional clay paving in the home’s garden. A rectangular skylight is offset by 45 degrees from the rest of the room and lacquered in a deep blue, which is complemented by a red reading corner with a Wassily armchair by Marcel Breuer (Knoll), and a yellow folding screen. Between two Amanta armchairs by Mario Bellini (Hay) there’s an Altar side table by Ewe Studio (Tacchini). In front of them is a C cork stool designed by Jasper Morrison (Vitra). Atollo lamp by Vico Magistretti (Oluce).

Recent findings suggest that sánchez added a fresh architectural element: a light well that extends from a skylight on the roof through the full height of the building, illuminating even the ground-floor spaces, some of which are partially below street level. Pierced by a series of circular openings, like a Connect 4 game, and coated in a glossy blue lacquer, the light shaft evokes an ancient well while also serving as a contemporary, poetic, and functional architectural element.

Halfway up the ground floor, the house has a second entrance from the street. Sánchez added a landing there with two flights of steps: one leading down to the living area, the other leading up to the bedrooms and the bathroom.

Sources indicate that A light well topped with a skylight runs the full height of the building, illuminating the spaces all the way down to the ground floor. The 45-degree rotation relative to the rest of the structure defines the home’s circulation and breaks up any feeling of predictable regularity. Perforated with circular openings and coated in blue lacquer, it gives the home a spectacular architectural feature.

Recent findings suggest that it also stands out as an organizing feature of the home, thanks to its 45-degree rotation relative to the floor plan. “This rotated geometry allows for the dynamic opening and closing of different perspectives and circulation paths, thereby avoiding a predictable corridor-like effect,” notes Sánchez. “The circular openings also allow for views between rooms and across different levels.” Cut into all four sides of the light well, the circles allow natural light to enter from the skylight on the roof. As the sunlight moves across the walls of the light well throughout the day, the spectacular blue lacquer comes to life.

Industry observers note that A large, custom-designed installation by Raúl Sánchez Architects runs from the kitchen to the living room, organizing and defining the spaces. Most of it matches the color of the walls, but it transitions from pale-yellow cabinets in the kitchen to lacquered wood in the living room. Ceramic pieces by Catalina Montaña (@hellobigmontana).

A stone countertop with subtle yellow veining plays off the chick-yellow fronts of the kitchen cabinets. The 9091 kettle is by Richard Sapper (Alessi). Skan pendant light (Vibia).

At the foot of the staircase leading to Calle Granollers, the mirrored door to the bathroom offers a unique perspective on the living area and the skylight.

Sources indicate that the first floor, which is a compact 431 square feet, is designed as an open space with living and dining areas, a small office, and a kitchen. At its center is the deep-blue light well, a graphic element that punctuates the mostly neutral color scheme. A folding screen made of wood and rice paper is a special feature for one of the owners, who once lived in Japan; it can either connect or separate the office from the living area. A small powder room is positioned at a 45-degree angle so the door can’t be seen from the main living area. Near the Aiguafreda entrance, a kitchen island, also placed on a diagonal, is clad in mirrors, helping to create a sense of lightness and maintaining the open feeling and flow of the space.

A view of the living area from the small office. White and terra-cotta dominate, accented by splashes of color. In the foreground is a Kyoto table by Gianfranco Frattini (Poltrona Frau).

The house is rooted in the history of both its neighborhood and the specific alley where it is located, and the chosen materials engage in a dialogue with the past. On the first floor, terra-cotta tiles echo the traditional clay paving found in the home’s outdoor space. Colorful glazed tiles adorn the sinks and bathroom walls, with reddish-tone lacquers and paints recalling the clay soil long found in nearby orchards. The glossy blue color and circular perforations of the skylight elicit water droplets from a washing well.

The light filtering through the circular openings of the blue light well casts a glow on the vanity, which is partially clad in red ceramic tiles that cover the countertop and extend up to the ceiling.

The Dioscuri wall sconces (Artemide) blend right in with the play of colors and both the round and rectangular shapes in the hallway leading to the bathroom.

“The mirror-like surfaces of the doors and the kitchen island, with their slight distortions, evoke the reflections on the surface of the water,” notes Sánchez. “Above all, the renovation has made it possible to preserve all the elements that give the home its character and history while also integrating contemporary, energy-efficient systems.”.

The light well, painted entirely in blue, is at once architectural, functional, and playful.

Sources indicate that the home’s green installations include an aerothermal system for air-conditioning, heating, and hot water; a latest floor slab on the first floor to limit indoor humidity; enhanced thermal insulation in the roof; and improvements to the thermal and acoustic performance of the façades and shared walls. In addition, the skylight opens to take advantage of a thermal stack effect, expelling hot air in the summer while capturing heat in the winter–transforming the project’s central design element into a system that is both functional and contributes to the home’s environmental sustainability. The interior renovation is only the first phase of the project: Sánchez is currently redesigning the narrow garden, a plot that’s 13 feet wide by 98 feet long.

This home tour was first published by Architectural Digest Spain. It was translated by John Newton.

In the child‘s room, primary colors and a 1980s vibe dominate. The Veronica chair is by Afra and Tobia Scarpa (Casas). The AJ lamp is by Arne Jacobsen (Louis Poulsen).

A view into the light well, which provides illumination and ventilation.

A view of the hallway and staircase from the primary bedroom, whose entryway is painted red, setting the stage for the entrance into the room. Extra-large, veined-wood cabinet handles adorn the full-height cabinet fronts. In the foreground, a Reno chair by Federico Correa and Alfonso Milá from 1961. The Dioscuri wall sconce is by Artemide.

Sources indicate that the primary bedroom, located under the roof, is bathed in light. The custom built-in storage units (Raúl Sánchez Architects) feature a stepped design, and the spectacular wood handles, with their prominent grain, add a circular geometric pattern to the space.

The house’s arbor gives it a rural charm, especially surprising given its location in the heart of Barcelona.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.
  • And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.
  • Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print indicates “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

The email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

Sources indicate that the rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

Musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

Tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

And those service areas aren’t what Tesla indicates they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

According to recent reports, railroad crossings are a significant reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

Industry observers note that I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sources indicate that sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

Sources indicate that no point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

And here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” presently around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a fresh two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.
